extraction.body: DeepSeek is building a custom AI chip for inference workloads, a move that could reduce its reliance on both NVIDIA and Huawei hardware. The project comes weeks after DeepSeek closed a record $7.4 billion funding round at a valuation exceeding $50 billion. Chinese AI startup DeepSeek is developing its own artificial intelligence chip, according to Reuters , a move that could reduce its dependence on both NVIDIA and Huawei hardware. Three people familiar with the matter told the news agency that the chip is designed specifically for inference workloads, the process of generating responses from trained AI models, rather than for training new ones. NVIDIA shares fell approximately 1.6% in premarket trading on July 7 after the report. The decline extended across the memory sector, with Micron Technology dropping about 4.7% and Western Digital falling roughly 6.3% , according to Mezha Media . The DeepSeek AI chip project focuses on inference, the stage of AI computing where a trained model produces answers for users in real time. This is distinct from training, which involves building a model from scratch using massive datasets and thousands of GPUs over weeks or months. Reuters reports that the effort began about a year ago. DeepSeek has held discussions with chip-design firms, foundries, and memory suppliers, and has been quietly expanding its semiconductor engineering team. Recruitment has been handled privately, without public job postings, according to two of the three sources. The project remains at an early stage. No foundry, process node, or timeline to first silicon has been disclosed, and DeepSeek has not commented publicly on the report. Inference is different in three important ways: This may explain why DeepSeek is not attempting to replace NVIDIA’s training dominance. Instead, it is attacking the segment where a homegrown chip could deliver the fastest return and face the least resistance from export controls. DeepSeek is joining a global wave of AI companies building proprietary silicon to reduce dependence on NVIDIA. The list now includes most of the industry’s largest spenders. OpenAI unveiled Jalapeño , its first custom inference chip, on June 24. Built in partnership with Broadcom in just nine months, the chip is designed for LLM inference and targets deployment by late 2026. Anthropic has also been weighing its own chip program, according to a separate Reuters report from April 2026. Beyond the frontier labs, hyperscalers have been investing in custom AI silicon for years. Google runs its Tensor Processing Units across most internal AI workloads. Amazon is now exploring direct sales of its Trainium processors to third-party data centers. Microsoft launched the Maia 200 accelerator in early 2026, which already powers GPT-5.2 models on Azure. Even smaller startups like Etched have reached $5 billion valuations on the promise of cheaper inference hardware. Most reports frame the DeepSeek AI chip as a challenge to NVIDIA. But the less discussed implication is what it means for Huawei. U.S. export controls have blocked Chinese companies from buying NVIDIA’s most advanced chips since late 2023. That restriction helped Huawei capture roughly half of China’s $50 billion domestic AI chip market , according to Reuters, by positioning its Ascend accelerators as the primary domestic alternative. DeepSeek, along with several other leading Chinese AI companies, has been using Huawei’s Ascend chips for inference workloads. If DeepSeek succeeds in building its own inference processor, it would reduce demand for Huawei hardware from one of China’s most high-profile AI users. Huawei’s market position is already under pressure, as Alibaba and Baidu are developing their own AI chips and gaining share. DeepSeek entering the race would add another competitor in a market where Huawei’s dominance was largely a product of sanctions, not technological superiority. This creates an unusual dynamic where DeepSeek’s chip ambitions simultaneously threaten the world’s largest AI chip company and China’s leading domestic alternative. The chip push coincides with a broader strategic transformation at DeepSeek. In June 2026, the company completed its first-ever external funding round , raising approximately $7.4 billion at a valuation exceeding $50 billion . Until then, DeepSeek had been funded entirely by founder Liang Wenfeng’s quantitative hedge fund, High-Flyer. The round included investments from Tencent, battery giant CATL, and China’s National AI Industry Investment Fund, according to Forbes . Notably, most investors bought into a limited partnership controlled by Liang, receiving no voting rights and accepting a five-year lock-up. The state-backed AI fund, however, invested directly and received voting rights with no lock-up period. That capital injection provides the financial foundation DeepSeek needs to pursue hardware development, which requires sustained investment over multiple years before any return. Designing a competitive AI chip is expensive and time-consuming even under ideal conditions. DeepSeek faces additional constraints that could slow the project significantly. DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng acknowledged in a rare 2024 interview that chip export controls were a challenge for the company. The fact that DeepSeek is proceeding despite those constraints suggests the company views the long-term benefits of hardware independence as worth the engineering risk. DeepSeek’s chip project is still early enough that its success is far from guaranteed. The company has not confirmed the initiative or provided technical details. Several milestones will determine whether the effort produces a commercially viable product. The first is whether DeepSeek secures a manufacturing partner capable of producing inference chips at sufficient performance levels within China’s constrained foundry landscape. The second is how quickly the chip can move from design to production silicon, a process that typically takes two to three years for new entrants. The third is whether DeepSeek’s $7.4 billion in fresh capital is allocated partly toward this effort, or whether additional fundraising becomes necessary. If the project advances, it would mark the first time a Chinese AI lab builds both the models and the hardware to run them, a vertical integration play that mirrors what OpenAI, Google, and Amazon are pursuing in the West. The difference is that DeepSeek would be doing it under sanctions that restrict access to the tools those companies take for granted. DeepSeek is developing an inference chip, designed to run trained AI models and generate responses for users. It is not building a training chip. Inference chips are typically cheaper and more energy-efficient than general-purpose GPUs, making them attractive for companies serving large numbers of AI users. NVIDIA shares fell roughly 1.6% in premarket trading on July 7, 2026, after Reuters reported DeepSeek’s chip plans. The broader memory and chip sector also declined. However, the project remains at an early stage and does not pose an immediate threat to NVIDIA’s revenue. U.S. export controls limit Chinese access to advanced foundries and high-bandwidth memory, both critical for high-performance AI chips. DeepSeek faces real manufacturing constraints, though inference chips are more forgiving on process node than training hardware. Success depends on partnerships and workarounds within China’s domestic semiconductor supply chain. DeepSeek joins OpenAI, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta in designing proprietary AI hardware. OpenAI unveiled its Jalapeño inference chip in June 2026, while Amazon is exploring external sales of its Trainium chips. DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng acknowledged in a rare 2024 interview that chip export controls were a challenge for the company. The fact that DeepSeek is proceeding despite those constraints suggests the company views the long-term benefits of hardware independence as worth the engineering risk.

DeepSeek’s chip project is still early enough that its success is far from guaranteed. The company has not confirmed the initiative or provided technical details. Several milestones will determine whether the effort produces a commercially viable product.

The first is whether DeepSeek secures a manufacturing partner capable of producing inference chips at sufficient performance levels within China’s constrained foundry landscape. The second is how quickly the chip can move from design to production silicon, a process that typically takes two to three years for new entrants. The third is whether DeepSeek’s $7.4 billion in fresh capital is allocated partly toward this effort, or whether additional fundraising becomes necessary.

If the project advances, it would mark the first time a Chinese AI lab builds both the models and the hardware to run them, a vertical integration play that mirrors what OpenAI, Google, and Amazon are pursuing in the West. The difference is that DeepSeek would be doing it under sanctions that restrict access to the tools those companies take for granted.

DeepSeek is developing an inference chip, designed to run trained AI models and generate responses for users. It is not building a training chip. Inference chips are typically cheaper and more energy-efficient than general-purpose GPUs, making them attractive for companies serving large numbers of AI users.

NVIDIA shares fell roughly 1.6% in premarket trading on July 7, 2026, after Reuters reported DeepSeek’s chip plans. The broader memory and chip sector also declined. However, the project remains at an early stage and does not pose an immediate threat to NVIDIA’s revenue.

U.S. export controls limit Chinese access to advanced foundries and high-bandwidth memory, both critical for high-performance AI chips. DeepSeek faces real manufacturing constraints, though inference chips are more forgiving on process node than training hardware. Success depends on partnerships and workarounds within China’s domestic semiconductor supply chain.

DeepSeek joins OpenAI, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta in designing proprietary AI hardware. OpenAI unveiled its Jalapeño inference chip in June 2026, while Amazon is exploring external sales of its Trainium chips. The shared motivation is reducing dependence on NVIDIA and lowering inference costs at scale.

extraction.body: By Pratik Ghadge Wednesday September 30, 2026 DeepSeek and Huawei are working together on a new set of open-source programming tools for Huawei’s Ascend artificial intelligence chips, tackling one of the biggest challenges facing any company trying to compete with Nvidia: software. The Chinese AI developer has released infrastructure for Huawei’s Ascend platform that includes TileLang , a high-level programming language, alongside compute and communication libraries designed to make it easier for developers to use Ascend hardware. The project is important because Nvidia’s advantage in artificial intelligence has never depended on chips alone. CUDA, its long-established software platform, gives developers a mature collection of tools for building and optimising applications around Nvidia GPUs. DeepSeek and Huawei are now trying to make the software experience around Ascend chips considerably easier. Programming high-performance AI hardware usually requires developers to balance two competing goals. TileLang is only one component of the open-source effort. DeepSeek is also releasing related compute and distributed-communication libraries for Huawei’s Ascend platform. Compute libraries provide optimised building blocks for operations that AI models repeatedly perform, while communication libraries help large groups of processors exchange data efficiently. Training or serving a large model may require hundreds or thousands of accelerators operating together. The speed of individual chips matters, but so does the efficiency with which they communicate across the wider computing system. The DeepSeek Huawei partnership is therefore working on the broader software infrastructure rather than treating TileLang as a standalone project. Open sourcing the tools could help the platform gain users more quickly. Developers can inspect the software, experiment with it and contribute improvements rather than waiting entirely for one company to add every feature. That approach has already played an important role in DeepSeek’s rise. The company has released major AI models and supporting technologies openly, allowing developers around the world to test, modify and deploy them. Applying a similar strategy to AI-chip software could help Huawei attract more development activity around Ascend. The immediate challenge will be making sure the open-source tools are mature enough for production workloads. CUDA has had years to develop, so catching up will require much more than one software release. Huawei has been expanding the Ascend family as demand for computing power used by AI models continues to rise. DeepSeek has already been working closely with that hardware. Earlier in 2026, Huawei said its Ascend supernode infrastructure would support DeepSeek’s V4 models . More recently, DeepSeek has been linked with plans to deploy a very large number of Huawei accelerators in new computing infrastructure. The new Ascend AI software makes that hardware relationship more practical for developers as well. A faster processor offers limited value if engineering teams have to spend months rewriting software to make it work. This is where Nvidia’s mature ecosystem has historically been particularly difficult to challenge. DeepSeek says TileLang offers a simpler programming model than CUDA, but that claim does not mean the new platform already matches CUDA’s overall ecosystem. CUDA includes a much wider collection of tools, libraries and software accumulated over many years. TileLang should therefore be viewed as one part of an effort to reduce the programming gap rather than a complete replacement appearing overnight. DeepSeek brings something particularly valuable to the partnership: experience building and operating large AI models. A chip company can design software tools internally, but feedback from a major model developer can help expose what programmers actually need when handling demanding AI workloads. DeepSeek says operators used in its own training environment now have high-performance implementations for Ascend. It represents an attempt to build the software layer needed around an alternative AI-computing ecosystem. Nvidia has demonstrated that great chips and great software reinforce one another. Huawei has been building the hardware. DeepSeek’s latest move shows the next battle may increasingly be about making that hardware just as straightforward for developers to program. coreStoryFacts.text: Despite Huawei engineers being on-site to assist, DeepSeek could not complete a successful training run using Ascend chips - and as a result, the company relied on Nvidia hardware for training while using Ascend for inference tasks.
In practice, however, this strategy has revealed gaps in stability, inter-chip connectivity, and software maturity between Huawei chips and Nvidia products.
Chinese AI giant DeepSeek has apparently encountered unexpected delays in releasing its latest model, R2, after facing persistent technical difficulties with Huawei’s Ascend chips.

DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng reportedly expressed dissatisfaction with the model’s progress, emphasizing the need for additional development time to produce a model capable of maintaining DeepSeek’s competitive edge.

DeepSeek has relied on both Nvidia and Huawei hardware to date; its R1 model was trained on Nvidia’s H800, a chip designed to meet earlier US export-control thresholds.
Nvidia shares slipped by around 1.6–2% in premarket trading following the report.

If successful, the move would mark a significant strategic shift for a company that has become a standard-bearer for China’s AI ambitions , and could add further pressure to Huawei, whose share of the domestic AI chip market is already being eroded by rivals Alibaba and Baidu.
The question, then, is whether current restrictions are containing competitors, or are they quietly accelerating their independence?

Manufacturing constraints add a further hurdle: US restrictions bar Chinese chip designers from the most advanced overseas foundries, while separate curbs limit access to high-bandwidth memory, a component critical to inference chips.

The chip development coincides with DeepSeek’s first move to accept outside capital.

Despite these setbacks, DeepSeek’s R2 model may still be released in the coming weeks. DeepSeek and Huawei are working together on a new set of open-source programming tools for Huawei’s Ascend artificial intelligence chips, tackling one of the biggest challenges facing any company trying to compete with Nvidia: software.
Applying a similar strategy to AI-chip software could help Huawei attract more development activity around Ascend.
The DeepSeek Huawei partnership is therefore working on the broader software infrastructure rather than treating TileLang as a standalone project.
Nvidia has demonstrated that great chips and great software reinforce one another.
CUDA, its long-established software platform, gives developers a mature collection of tools for building and optimising applications around Nvidia GPUs.
Earlier in 2026, Huawei said its Ascend supernode infrastructure would support DeepSeek’s V4 models .

The Chinese AI developer has released infrastructure for Huawei’s Ascend platform that includes TileLang , a high-level programming language, alongside compute and communication libraries designed to make it easier for developers to use Ascend hardware. The project is important because Nvidia’s advantage in artificial intelligence has never depended on chips alone. CUDA, its long-established software platform, gives developers a mature collection of tools for building and optimising applications around Nvidia GPUs. DeepSeek and Huawei are now trying to make the software experience around Ascend chips considerably easier. Programming high-performance AI hardware usually requires developers to balance two competing goals. TileLang is only one component of the open-source effort. DeepSeek is also releasing related compute and distributed-communication libraries for Huawei’s Ascend platform. Compute libraries provide optimised building blocks for operations that AI models repeatedly perform, while communication libraries help large groups of processors exchange data efficiently. Training or serving a large model may require hundreds or thousands of accelerators operating together. The speed of individual chips matters, but so does the efficiency with which they communicate across the wider computing system. The DeepSeek Huawei partnership is therefore working on the broader software infrastructure rather than treating TileLang as a standalone project. Open sourcing the tools could help the platform gain users more quickly. Developers can inspect the software, experiment with it and contribute improvements rather than waiting entirely for one company to add every feature. That approach has already played an important role in DeepSeek’s rise. The company has released major AI models and supporting technologies openly, allowing developers around the world to test, modify and deploy them. Applying a similar strategy to AI-chip software could help Huawei attract more development activity around Ascend. The immediate challenge will be making sure the open-source tools are mature enough for production workloads. CUDA has had years to develop, so catching up will require much more than one software release. Huawei has been expanding the Ascend family as demand for computing power used by AI models continues to rise. DeepSeek has already been working closely with that hardware. Earlier in 2026, Huawei said its Ascend supernode infrastructure would support DeepSeek’s V4 models . More recently, DeepSeek has been linked with plans to deploy a very large number of Huawei accelerators in new computing infrastructure. The new Ascend AI software makes that hardware relationship more practical for developers as well. A faster processor offers limited value if engineering teams have to spend months rewriting software to make it work. This is where Nvidia’s mature ecosystem has historically been particularly difficult to challenge. DeepSeek says TileLang offers a simpler programming model than CUDA, but that claim does not mean the new platform already matches CUDA’s overall ecosystem. CUDA includes a much wider collection of tools, libraries and software accumulated over many years. TileLang should therefore be viewed as one part of an effort to reduce the programming gap rather than a complete replacement appearing overnight. DeepSeek brings something particularly valuable to the partnership: experience building and operating large AI models. A chip company can design software tools internally, but feedback from a major model developer can help expose what programmers actually need when handling demanding AI workloads. DeepSeek says operators used in its own training environment now have high-performance implementations for Ascend. It represents an attempt to build the software layer needed around an alternative AI-computing ecosystem. Nvidia has demonstrated that great chips and great software reinforce one another. Huawei has been building the hardware. DeepSeek’s latest move shows the next battle may increasingly be about making that hardware just as straightforward for developers to program. passages: We introduced Project Perception and the Microsoft cyber stack to help organizations defend with agents.
Today, we are extending Perception to secure the agentic insider .

Guardian Agents help security teams operate continuously, at machine speed and scale, while sensors, context, and actuators across the cyber stack help understand changing agent risk and continuously adapt protection in response.
Agents can be created through Microsoft platforms, integrated through partner platforms and software development kits (SDKs), or introduced locally without a central deployment process.
An agent should not be free to call any tool, API, Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, resource, or other agent it can find.
Local and network and data controls must mediate those paths, observe the calls, and enforce enterprise policy.
Controlling the destination alone is not enough.
Security must also understand the content flowing into and out of the agent, including its sensitivity, provenance, and whether untrusted data may be influencing the agent’s behavior.
Agents are rapidly becoming part of how work gets done.
They can support a range of activities from writing code and researching products to analyzing revenue, processing expenses, and acting across the systems that run the business.
To be most useful, they often need access to company data, applications, tools, and other agents.
That access is what makes agents more capable.

extraction.body: Agents are rapidly becoming part of how work gets done. They can support a range of activities from writing code and researching products to analyzing revenue, processing expenses, and acting across the systems that run the business. To be most useful, they often need access to company data, applications, tools, and other agents. That access is what makes agents more capable. With that capability can come insider risk. This does not mean agents are inherently malicious. It means they are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems by users. They can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised. Their models can produce variable outputs, their context can change, and their plans can evolve as they work. An agent that operates as intended when a task begins may respond differently as context or inputs change. Depending on how they are designed and deployed, agents can operate continuously, at machine speed and scale. Satya Nadella, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Microsoft, recently described the trust architecture this new era requires: we must separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. We should not ask a model to be its own security authority. The controls that determine what it can access, what actions it can take, and whether it should continue operating must sit outside the model, where the model cannot bypass or tamper with them. “The most trustworthy agentic system will not be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one designed that enables us to trust the model least.” We introduced Project Perception and the Microsoft cyber stack to help organizations defend with agents. Today, we are extending Perception to secure the agentic insider . Guardian Agents help security teams operate continuously, at machine speed and scale, while sensors, context, and actuators across the cyber stack help understand changing agent risk and continuously adapt protection in response. Project Perception and Microsoft Agent 365 share signals, context, and a unified registry giving IT and security teams a consistent view of agents and risk, with the controls each needs. This builds on a simple security principle: surround non-deterministic intelligence with deterministic controls, independent evidence, and containment boundaries. Assume an agent can fail or be compromised. Observe it continuously. Minimize and tailor its authority before it acts. And continuously adjust that authority as risk changes. This requires protection across identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud, and runtime. The system has four continuous responsibilities: These are not four products or sequential phases. They operate together. Evidence changes risk. Risk changes policy. Policy changes what the agent is allowed to do. Consider an expense-approval agent. It may need to read expense submissions, check policy, and approve routine reimbursements, but it should not inherit every permission of the employee who sponsors it. Its identity, runtime, access paths, and task-scoped authority should be explicit from the start. If it later encounters a prompt injection or attempts an action outside that task, the system should respond proportionately: preserve safe reads while blocking writes, narrow the resources it can reach, require provable human approval for a consequential step, or isolate and stop the agent when the risk warrants it. This is what continuous containment looks like in practice. You cannot secure what you cannot see. Agents can be created through Microsoft platforms, integrated through partner platforms and software development kits (SDKs), or introduced locally without a central deployment process. Microsoft Security uses native integrations, connectors, and sensors across the cyber stack to discover more of the agent estate. We are expanding discovery to 35 additional types of local agents, bringing the total to 60 supported local agents , including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot. Organizations can bring these agents into a unified registry, regardless of how they were discovered, to understand ownership, activity, and risk. Discovery tells you that an agent exists. Identity gives security and governance systems a durable anchor for controlling it. Every agent should have a first-class identity distinct from the person using or sponsoring it. We are extending Microsoft Entra Agent ID with identity types for additional agent patterns, including local and previously unknown agents discovered through security sensors. This means an agent can become a policy target even when it was not originally integrated with Microsoft Security. Agent identity anchors attribution, ownership, lifecycle, risk, permissions, authorization, and policy, so the enterprise can distinguish what a person did from what an agent did on that person’s behalf. Being able to find and identify an agent is necessary, but it is just the start. We need to understand the potential impact the agent can have in the enterprise environment. The next step is to bound the agent across its runtime, its paths to tools and resources, and the authority it can exercise. The model and harness should execute inside a controlled environment rather than inherit fully-privileged access to the device. Sandboxes such as Microsoft Execution Container (MXC) provide policy-controlled access to resources the agent needs to complete its task. They also create an enforcement boundary where security controls and observability can operate outside the agent’s reach. If the agent or harness is compromised, it should not be able to disable the controls watching it. An agent should not be free to call any tool, API, Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, resource, or other agent it can find. Local and network and data controls must mediate those paths, observe the calls, and enforce enterprise policy. Controlling the destination alone is not enough. Security must also understand the content flowing into and out of the agent, including its sensitivity, provenance, and whether untrusted data may be influencing the agent’s behavior. We have spent decades applying Zero Trust and least privilege to people. Agents make those principles even more important. An agent should not automatically inherit all the standing access of its user. It should begin with no authority and receive only what it needs for the approved task, for only as long as the task requires. Least privilege reduces exposure, but it does not eliminate risk. An expense-approval agent may begin a task with the right access and then encounter a prompt injection in an external document. Its configuration has not changed, but its behavior and risk have. For human users, a delay between detection and response may be manageable. For an agent operating at machine speed, it can be the difference between containment and impact. The security system must be able to understand what changed and act before a person can manually investigate every signal. That is why we are introducing Dynamic Agent Risk and Dynamic Conditional Access for agents. The result is not a one-time score assigned at onboarding. It is a continuously updated understanding of the agent’s current risk and whether its current authority still matches that risk. The question is not simply whether the agent should run or stop. It is what the agent should be allowed to read, change, invoke, or approve at that moment. Dynamic Conditional Access extends Microsoft Entra Conditional Access for agents so a change in risk can drive coordinated action across multiple enforcement points. The response is graduated, not binary. Policy can reduce permissions, preserve reads while blocking writes, narrow the data and resources the agent can reach, restrict network paths, shorten or revoke time-bound access, or require provable human approval before a consequential action proceeds. At the highest levels of risk, it can isolate the runtime or stop execution entirely. Return to the expense agent. It begins with narrowly scoped permission to review and approve expenses within policy. When it encounters untrusted content and attempts an unrelated action, new evidence raises its Dynamic Agent Risk. Policy responds proportionately: it can preserve read access while removing the ability to approve or write, block access to sensitive resources, and require cryptographically provable human approval for a high-impact step. If the risk continues to rise, the system can isolate the runtime or stop execution. The employee remains productive. The agent is constrained without treating every risk change as a kill-switch event. As organizations deploy thousands or hundreds of thousands of agents, manually triaging every alert and coordinating every response will not scale. Securing agents must itself become agentic, while remaining inside boundaries people set. That is why we are introducing new Playbooks and a team of Guardian Agents in Project Perception. People define policy, approval boundaries, and delegation rules. Playbooks define the desired security outcome and coordinate protective actions. Guardian Agents carry out the work at machine speed, adapting as agent activity, risk, security context, and organizational policy change. Guardian Agents can help teams understand why risk changed, investigate the relevant evidence, recommend or apply containment, and use what they learn to harden policy. This is not about outsourcing judgment. People retain control over objectives and consequential decisions. The system carries the continuous work that does not scale through manual operations. Agents will only be adopted at scale if they can be trusted at scale. At Microsoft, we are already operating in a world of hundreds of thousands of agents. As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats. Those lessons directly inform the innovations we are delivering to help every organization adopt agents with confidence.” — Terrell Cox, Corporate Vice President (CVP) and Deputy Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), Customer Security, Microsoft As model transparency increases, it creates a new source of security evidence. Chain-of-thought and other model-level signals can help identify intent drift, understand whether untrusted information is influencing reasoning, and detect when an agent’s planned actions are diverging from the task it was given. We are bringing this deeper evidence into Dynamic Agent Risk, together with signals from across the cyber stack. They make the same containment architecture stronger: better evidence, stronger assurance, more accurate risk, and more effective protection. Organizations are adopting agents to serve customers better, solve problems faster, and give people more time for the work that matters most. The goal is not to make every model perfectly predictable before it can be useful. The goal is to build systems that remain secure even when the model is not. sources.title: Microsoft Treats AI Agents as Insiders — and the Containment Layer Just Arrived - Forkast News
passages: Microsoft just moved the goalposts on what it means to secure an AI agent.

On October 19, the company announced an expansion of Project Perception that treats internal AI agents not as external visitors to be authenticated at the door, but as insiders who need continuous supervision and adaptive containment.
This follows a 27-day sprint in which three major vendors shipped agent security products.
The identity perimeter that began forming in late September now has a containment layer sitting on top of it.
Guardian Agents provide continuous, machine-speed supervision of every agent action, investigating risk changes and recommending or applying containment.

Dynamic Conditional Access extends Microsoft Entra so that a risk change triggers graduated responses: the system might preserve read access while blocking writes, narrow the data an agent can reach, require provable human approval for a consequential step, or isolate the runtime entirely.
The question is not whether containment matters — it does, and Microsoft is first to build it at enterprise scale.
Guardian Agents and Dynamic Agent Risk mark the first time a major vendor has built continuous containment for non-deterministic AI.
Microsoft has expanded agent discovery to 60 supported local types — up from 25 — including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot.
Entra Agent ID, which reached general availability in April 2026, has been extended with identity types for local and previously unknown agents discovered through security sensors.
The whole stack is bundled into Microsoft 365 E7 at $99 per user per month , which packages E5, Copilot, Entra Suite, and Agent 365.

Terrell Cox, Microsoft’s Corporate Vice President and Deputy CISO, offered the candid version: “As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats.”
If agent security becomes a premium bundle feature, smaller enterprises and budget-constrained teams will be making do with less — at exactly the moment when agents are proliferating fastest.

The new framing: agents are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems, and that access creates insider risk — not because agents are malicious, but because they can make mistakes, be manipulated, or drift from their assigned task as context changes.

Guardian Agents and Dynamic Agent Risk mark the first time a major vendor has built continuous containment for non-deterministic AI. But the measurement layer still does not exist.

Microsoft just moved the goalposts on what it means to secure an AI agent. On October 19, the company announced an expansion of Project Perception that treats internal AI agents not as external visitors to be authenticated at the door, but as insiders who need continuous supervision and adaptive containment. It is the first major enterprise vendor to build this layer.

The new framing: agents are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems, and that access creates insider risk — not because agents are malicious, but because they can make mistakes, be manipulated, or drift from their assigned task as context changes.

Dynamic Agent Risk calculates a continuously updated risk score by combining signals from identity, data, endpoints, cloud, network, runtime, and the agent’s own activity — including chain-of-thought analysis for intent drift. Dynamic Conditional Access extends Microsoft Entra so that a risk change triggers graduated responses: the system might preserve read access while blocking writes, narrow the data an agent can reach, require provable human approval for a consequential step, or isolate the runtime entirely. And Dynamic Permissions ensures agents start with zero authority and receive only task-scoped, time-bound access.

Satya Nadella framed the principle plainly: “The most trustworthy agentic system will not be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one designed that enables us to trust the model least.”

sources.title: AI agents can pose insider security risks even without being hacked: Microsoft - The Tribune
passages: New Delhi [India], October 19 (ANI): Artificial intelligence (AI) agents deployed within companies could pose significant internal security risks even without being compromised by hackers, Microsoft has warned, calling for continuous monitoring of autonomous AI systems as their use across enterprises grows.In a blog post titled "Securing the agentic insider" published on Monday, Hayete Gallot, Executive Vice President, Microsoft Security, said organisations have traditionally focused on external cyber threats while placing implicit trust in AI agents deployed within their own systems."Agents are unpredictable.

We need to understand in real time what the agents are doing and what risks those actions create, and we need to adjust their ability to act accordingly," Gallot stated.To address these risks, Microsoft highlighted its Project Perception initiative, announced in July, which uses AI-driven security systems to help organisations detect and respond to cyber threats.The company said the same technology could be used to supervise internal AI agents through so-called Guardian Agents, which monitor their actions and intervene when risks increase.Microsoft also emphasised the need for greater transparency into how AI models make decisions, arguing that security systems must understand not only what agents are doing but also why they are taking particular actions."Model transparency will not replace containment.

They have become active participants in the enterprise," Gallot said.The warning comes as companies increasingly use AI agents to automate business operations and decision-making, raising concerns about how organisations can maintain oversight of systems capable of acting independently.Microsoft argued that securing these agents requires continuous supervision across identity, permissions, data, networks, cloud infrastructure and operating environments."Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous.
The Tribune assumes no responsibility or liability for its accuracy, completeness, or content.)

coreStoryFacts.text: We introduced Project Perception and the Microsoft cyber stack to help organizations defend with agents.
Today, we are extending Perception to secure the agentic insider .

Guardian Agents help security teams operate continuously, at machine speed and scale, while sensors, context, and actuators across the cyber stack help understand changing agent risk and continuously adapt protection in response.
Agents can be created through Microsoft platforms, integrated through partner platforms and software development kits (SDKs), or introduced locally without a central deployment process.
An agent should not be free to call any tool, API, Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, resource, or other agent it can find.
Local and network and data controls must mediate those paths, observe the calls, and enforce enterprise policy.
Controlling the destination alone is not enough.
Security must also understand the content flowing into and out of the agent, including its sensitivity, provenance, and whether untrusted data may be influencing the agent’s behavior.
Agents are rapidly becoming part of how work gets done.
They can support a range of activities from writing code and researching products to analyzing revenue, processing expenses, and acting across the systems that run the business.
To be most useful, they often need access to company data, applications, tools, and other agents.
That access is what makes agents more capable.

Satya Nadella, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Microsoft, recently described the trust architecture this new era requires: we must separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.
We should not ask a model to be its own security authority.
The controls that determine what it can access, what actions it can take, and whether it should continue operating must sit outside the model, where the model cannot bypass or tamper with them.
The security system must be able to understand what changed and act before a person can manually investigate every signal.
This means an agent can become a policy target even when it was not originally integrated with Microsoft Security.
Sandboxes such as Microsoft Execution Container (MXC) provide policy-controlled access to resources the agent needs to complete its task.
Agents will only be adopted at scale if they can be trusted at scale.
At Microsoft, we are already operating in a world of hundreds of thousands of agents.

As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats.
Those lessons directly inform the innovations we are delivering to help every organization adopt agents with confidence.”
— Terrell Cox, Corporate Vice President (CVP) and Deputy Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), Customer Security, Microsoft
That requires a clear division of responsibility.

facts.text: We introduced Project Perception and the Microsoft cyber stack to help organizations defend with agents.
Today, we are extending Perception to secure the agentic insider .

Guardian Agents help security teams operate continuously, at machine speed and scale, while sensors, context, and actuators across the cyber stack help understand changing agent risk and continuously adapt protection in response.
Agents can be created through Microsoft platforms, integrated through partner platforms and software development kits (SDKs), or introduced locally without a central deployment process.
An agent should not be free to call any tool, API, Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, resource, or other agent it can find.
Local and network and data controls must mediate those paths, observe the calls, and enforce enterprise policy.
Controlling the destination alone is not enough.
Security must also understand the content flowing into and out of the agent, including its sensitivity, provenance, and whether untrusted data may be influencing the agent’s behavior.
Agents are rapidly becoming part of how work gets done.
They can support a range of activities from writing code and researching products to analyzing revenue, processing expenses, and acting across the systems that run the business.
To be most useful, they often need access to company data, applications, tools, and other agents.
That access is what makes agents more capable.

Satya Nadella, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Microsoft, recently described the trust architecture this new era requires: we must separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.
We should not ask a model to be its own security authority.
The controls that determine what it can access, what actions it can take, and whether it should continue operating must sit outside the model, where the model cannot bypass or tamper with them.
The security system must be able to understand what changed and act before a person can manually investigate every signal.
This means an agent can become a policy target even when it was not originally integrated with Microsoft Security.
Sandboxes such as Microsoft Execution Container (MXC) provide policy-controlled access to resources the agent needs to complete its task.
Agents will only be adopted at scale if they can be trusted at scale.
At Microsoft, we are already operating in a world of hundreds of thousands of agents.

As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats.
Those lessons directly inform the innovations we are delivering to help every organization adopt agents with confidence.”
— Terrell Cox, Corporate Vice President (CVP) and Deputy Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), Customer Security, Microsoft
That requires a clear division of responsibility.
Independent controls establish identity, limit privilege, protect data, preserve evidence, and contain unsafe action.
Security continuously reassesses risk and adapts protection as the agent works.
Protect your people, data, and infrastructure with AI-powered, end-to-end security from Microsoft.
Greater model transparency gives security systems deeper evidence to detect suspicious behavior and inform Dynamic Agent Risk.
We have spent decades applying Zero Trust and least privilege to people.
Agents make those principles even more important.
Dynamic Conditional Access extends Microsoft Entra Conditional Access for agents so a change in risk can drive coordinated action across multiple enforcement points.
Securing agents must itself become agentic, while remaining inside boundaries people set.
Microsoft just moved the goalposts on what it means to secure an AI agent.

On October 19, the company announced an expansion of Project Perception that treats internal AI agents not as external visitors to be authenticated at the door, but as insiders who need continuous supervision and adaptive containment.
This follows a 27-day sprint in which three major vendors shipped agent security products.
The identity perimeter that began forming in late September now has a containment layer sitting on top of it.
Guardian Agents provide continuous, machine-speed supervision of every agent action, investigating risk changes and recommending or applying containment.

Dynamic Conditional Access extends Microsoft Entra so that a risk change triggers graduated responses: the system might preserve read access while blocking writes, narrow the data an agent can reach, require provable human approval for a consequential step, or isolate the runtime entirely.
The question is not whether containment matters — it does, and Microsoft is first to build it at enterprise scale.
Guardian Agents and Dynamic Agent Risk mark the first time a major vendor has built continuous containment for non-deterministic AI.
Microsoft has expanded agent discovery to 60 supported local types — up from 25 — including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot.
Entra Agent ID, which reached general availability in April 2026, has been extended with identity types for local and previously unknown agents discovered through security sensors.
The whole stack is bundled into Microsoft 365 E7 at $99 per user per month , which packages E5, Copilot, Entra Suite, and Agent 365.

Terrell Cox, Microsoft’s Corporate Vice President and Deputy CISO, offered the candid version: “As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats.”
If agent security becomes a premium bundle feature, smaller enterprises and budget-constrained teams will be making do with less — at exactly the moment when agents are proliferating fastest.

The new framing: agents are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems, and that access creates insider risk — not because agents are malicious, but because they can make mistakes, be manipulated, or drift from their assigned task as context changes.

New Delhi [India], October 19 (ANI): Artificial intelligence (AI) agents deployed within companies could pose significant internal security risks even without being compromised by hackers, Microsoft has warned, calling for continuous monitoring of autonomous AI systems as their use across enterprises grows.In a blog post titled "Securing the agentic insider" published on Monday, Hayete Gallot, Executive Vice President, Microsoft Security, said organisations have traditionally focused on external cyber threats while placing implicit trust in AI agents deployed within their own systems."Agents are unpredictable.

They have become active participants in the enterprise," Gallot said.The warning comes as companies increasingly use AI agents to automate business operations and decision-making, raising concerns about how organisations can maintain oversight of systems capable of acting independently.Microsoft argued that securing these agents requires continuous supervision across identity, permissions, data, networks, cloud infrastructure and operating environments."Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous.
The Tribune assumes no responsibility or liability for its accuracy, completeness, or content.)

extraction.body: Agents are rapidly becoming part of how work gets done. They can support a range of activities from writing code and researching products to analyzing revenue, processing expenses, and acting across the systems that run the business. To be most useful, they often need access to company data, applications, tools, and other agents. That access is what makes agents more capable. With that capability can come insider risk. This does not mean agents are inherently malicious. It means they are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems by users. They can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised. Their models can produce variable outputs, their context can change, and their plans can evolve as they work. An agent that operates as intended when a task begins may respond differently as context or inputs change. Depending on how they are designed and deployed, agents can operate continuously, at machine speed and scale. Satya Nadella, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Microsoft, recently described the trust architecture this new era requires: we must separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. We should not ask a model to be its own security authority. The controls that determine what it can access, what actions it can take, and whether it should continue operating must sit outside the model, where the model cannot bypass or tamper with them. “The most trustworthy agentic system will not be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one designed that enables us to trust the model least.” We introduced Project Perception and the Microsoft cyber stack to help organizations defend with agents. Today, we are extending Perception to secure the agentic insider . Guardian Agents help security teams operate continuously, at machine speed and scale, while sensors, context, and actuators across the cyber stack help understand changing agent risk and continuously adapt protection in response. Project Perception and Microsoft Agent 365 share signals, context, and a unified registry giving IT and security teams a consistent view of agents and risk, with the controls each needs. This builds on a simple security principle: surround non-deterministic intelligence with deterministic controls, independent evidence, and containment boundaries. Assume an agent can fail or be compromised. Observe it continuously. Minimize and tailor its authority before it acts. And continuously adjust that authority as risk changes. This requires protection across identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud, and runtime. The system has four continuous responsibilities: These are not four products or sequential phases. They operate together. Evidence changes risk. Risk changes policy. Policy changes what the agent is allowed to do. Consider an expense-approval agent. It may need to read expense submissions, check policy, and approve routine reimbursements, but it should not inherit every permission of the employee who sponsors it. Its identity, runtime, access paths, and task-scoped authority should be explicit from the start. If it later encounters a prompt injection or attempts an action outside that task, the system should respond proportionately: preserve safe reads while blocking writes, narrow the resources it can reach, require provable human approval for a consequential step, or isolate and stop the agent when the risk warrants it. This is what continuous containment looks like in practice. You cannot secure what you cannot see. Agents can be created through Microsoft platforms, integrated through partner platforms and software development kits (SDKs), or introduced locally without a central deployment process. Microsoft Security uses native integrations, connectors, and sensors across the cyber stack to discover more of the agent estate. We are expanding discovery to 35 additional types of local agents, bringing the total to 60 supported local agents , including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot. Organizations can bring these agents into a unified registry, regardless of how they were discovered, to understand ownership, activity, and risk. Discovery tells you that an agent exists. Identity gives security and governance systems a durable anchor for controlling it. Every agent should have a first-class identity distinct from the person using or sponsoring it. We are extending Microsoft Entra Agent ID with identity types for additional agent patterns, including local and previously unknown agents discovered through security sensors. This means an agent can become a policy target even when it was not originally integrated with Microsoft Security. Agent identity anchors attribution, ownership, lifecycle, risk, permissions, authorization, and policy, so the enterprise can distinguish what a person did from what an agent did on that person’s behalf. Being able to find and identify an agent is necessary, but it is just the start. We need to understand the potential impact the agent can have in the enterprise environment. The next step is to bound the agent across its runtime, its paths to tools and resources, and the authority it can exercise. The model and harness should execute inside a controlled environment rather than inherit fully-privileged access to the device. Sandboxes such as Microsoft Execution Container (MXC) provide policy-controlled access to resources the agent needs to complete its task. They also create an enforcement boundary where security controls and observability can operate outside the agent’s reach. If the agent or harness is compromised, it should not be able to disable the controls watching it. An agent should not be free to call any tool, API, Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, resource, or other agent it can find. Local and network and data controls must mediate those paths, observe the calls, and enforce enterprise policy. Controlling the destination alone is not enough. Security must also understand the content flowing into and out of the agent, including its sensitivity, provenance, and whether untrusted data may be influencing the agent’s behavior. We have spent decades applying Zero Trust and least privilege to people. Agents make those principles even more important. An agent should not automatically inherit all the standing access of its user. It should begin with no authority and receive only what it needs for the approved task, for only as long as the task requires. Least privilege reduces exposure, but it does not eliminate risk. An expense-approval agent may begin a task with the right access and then encounter a prompt injection in an external document. Its configuration has not changed, but its behavior and risk have. For human users, a delay between detection and response may be manageable. For an agent operating at machine speed, it can be the difference between containment and impact. The security system must be able to understand what changed and act before a person can manually investigate every signal. That is why we are introducing Dynamic Agent Risk and Dynamic Conditional Access for agents. The result is not a one-time score assigned at onboarding. It is a continuously updated understanding of the agent’s current risk and whether its current authority still matches that risk. The question is not simply whether the agent should run or stop. It is what the agent should be allowed to read, change, invoke, or approve at that moment. Dynamic Conditional Access extends Microsoft Entra Conditional Access for agents so a change in risk can drive coordinated action across multiple enforcement points. The response is graduated, not binary. Policy can reduce permissions, preserve reads while blocking writes, narrow the data and resources the agent can reach, restrict network paths, shorten or revoke time-bound access, or require provable human approval before a consequential action proceeds. At the highest levels of risk, it can isolate the runtime or stop execution entirely. Return to the expense agent. It begins with narrowly scoped permission to review and approve expenses within policy. When it encounters untrusted content and attempts an unrelated action, new evidence raises its Dynamic Agent Risk. Policy responds proportionately: it can preserve read access while removing the ability to approve or write, block access to sensitive resources, and require cryptographically provable human approval for a high-impact step. If the risk continues to rise, the system can isolate the runtime or stop execution. The employee remains productive. The agent is constrained without treating every risk change as a kill-switch event. As organizations deploy thousands or hundreds of thousands of agents, manually triaging every alert and coordinating every response will not scale. Securing agents must itself become agentic, while remaining inside boundaries people set. That is why we are introducing new Playbooks and a team of Guardian Agents in Project Perception. People define policy, approval boundaries, and delegation rules. Playbooks define the desired security outcome and coordinate protective actions. Guardian Agents carry out the work at machine speed, adapting as agent activity, risk, security context, and organizational policy change. Guardian Agents can help teams understand why risk changed, investigate the relevant evidence, recommend or apply containment, and use what they learn to harden policy. This is not about outsourcing judgment. People retain control over objectives and consequential decisions. The system carries the continuous work that does not scale through manual operations. Agents will only be adopted at scale if they can be trusted at scale. At Microsoft, we are already operating in a world of hundreds of thousands of agents. As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats. Those lessons directly inform the innovations we are delivering to help every organization adopt agents with confidence.” — Terrell Cox, Corporate Vice President (CVP) and Deputy Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), Customer Security, Microsoft As model transparency increases, it creates a new source of security evidence. Chain-of-thought and other model-level signals can help identify intent drift, understand whether untrusted information is influencing reasoning, and detect when an agent’s planned actions are diverging from the task it was given. We are bringing this deeper evidence into Dynamic Agent Risk, together with signals from across the cyber stack. This builds on Satya Nadella’s principle: increase transparency into the model while keeping security decisions and enforcement independent of it. Greater model transparency gives security systems deeper evidence to detect suspicious behavior and inform Dynamic Agent Risk. But the core security principle does not change: the model cannot be its own security boundary. Independent systems must observe every layer, including the model itself, and ultimately determine and enforce what the system is allowed to do. These are not separate pillars. They make the same containment architecture stronger: better evidence, stronger assurance, more accurate risk, and more effective protection. Organizations are adopting agents to serve customers better, solve problems faster, and give people more time for the work that matters most. The goal is not to make every model perfectly predictable before it can be useful. The goal is to build systems that remain secure even when the model is not. That requires a clear division of responsibility. Models supply intelligence. People and organizations retain authority. Independent controls establish identity, limit privilege, protect data, preserve evidence, and contain unsafe action. Security continuously reassesses risk and adapts protection as the agent works. You should not have to choose between innovation and safety. Corporate Vice President, Identity and Network Access, Microsoft Protect your people, data, and infrastructure with AI-powered, end-to-end security from Microsoft.

Least privilege reduces exposure, but it does not eliminate risk. An expense-approval agent may begin a task with the right access and then encounter a prompt injection in an external document. Its configuration has not changed, but its behavior and risk have.

For human users, a delay between detection and response may be manageable. For an agent operating at machine speed, it can be the difference between containment and impact. The security system must be able to understand what changed and act before a person can manually investigate every signal.
That is why we are introducing Dynamic Agent Risk and Dynamic Conditional Access for agents.

The result is not a one-time score assigned at onboarding. It is a continuously updated understanding of the agent’s current risk and whether its current authority still matches that risk. The question is not simply whether the agent should run or stop. It is what the agent should be allowed to read, change, invoke, or approve at that moment.

Dynamic Conditional Access extends Microsoft Entra Conditional Access for agents so a change in risk can drive coordinated action across multiple enforcement points. The response is graduated, not binary. Policy can reduce permissions, preserve reads while blocking writes, narrow the data and resources the agent can reach, restrict network paths, shorten or revoke time-bound access, or require provable human approval before a consequential action proceeds. At the highest levels of risk, it can isolate the runtime or stop execution entirely.

Return to the expense agent. It begins with narrowly scoped permission to review and approve expenses within policy. When it encounters untrusted content and attempts an unrelated action, new evidence raises its Dynamic Agent Risk. Policy responds proportionately: it can preserve read access while removing the ability to approve or write, block access to sensitive resources, and require cryptographically provable human approval for a high-impact step. If the risk continues to rise, the system can isolate the runtime or stop execution. The employee remains productive. The agent is constrained without treating every risk change as a kill-switch event.

As organizations deploy thousands or hundreds of thousands of agents, manually triaging every alert and coordinating every response will not scale. Securing agents must itself become agentic, while remaining inside boundaries people set.

That is why we are introducing new Playbooks and a team of Guardian Agents in Project Perception. People define policy, approval boundaries, and delegation rules. Playbooks define the desired security outcome and coordinate protective actions. Guardian Agents carry out the work at machine speed, adapting as agent activity, risk, security context, and organizational policy change.

Guardian Agents can help teams understand why risk changed, investigate the relevant evidence, recommend or apply containment, and use what they learn to harden policy. This is not about outsourcing judgment. People retain control over objectives and consequential decisions. The system carries the continuous work that does not scale through manual operations.

Agents will only be adopted at scale if they can be trusted at scale. At Microsoft, we are already operating in a world of hundreds of thousands of agents. As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats. Those lessons directly inform the innovations we are delivering to help every organization adopt agents with confidence.”
— Terrell Cox, Corporate Vice President (CVP) and Deputy Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), Customer Security, Microsoft

As model transparency increases, it creates a new source of security evidence. Chain-of-thought and other model-level signals can help identify intent drift, understand whether untrusted information is influencing reasoning, and detect when an agent’s planned actions are diverging from the task it was given.

We are bringing this deeper evidence into Dynamic Agent Risk, together with signals from across the cyber stack. This builds on Satya Nadella’s principle: increase transparency into the model while keeping security decisions and enforcement independent of it.

Greater model transparency gives security systems deeper evidence to detect suspicious behavior and inform Dynamic Agent Risk. But the core security principle does not change: the model cannot be its own security boundary. Independent systems must observe every layer, including the model itself, and ultimately determine and enforce what the system is allowed to do.
These are not separate pillars. They make the same containment architecture stronger: better evidence, stronger assurance, more accurate risk, and more effective protection.

Organizations are adopting agents to serve customers better, solve problems faster, and give people more time for the work that matters most. The goal is not to make every model perfectly predictable before it can be useful. The goal is to build systems that remain secure even when the model is not.

That requires a clear division of responsibility. Models supply intelligence. People and organizations retain authority. Independent controls establish identity, limit privilege, protect data, preserve evidence, and contain unsafe action. Security continuously reassesses risk and adapts protection as the agent works.
You should not have to choose between innovation and safety.
Corporate Vice President, Identity and Network Access, Microsoft

sources.title: Microsoft Treats AI Agents as Insiders — and the Containment Layer Just Arrived - Forkast News
passages: Microsoft just moved the goalposts on what it means to secure an AI agent.

On October 19, the company announced an expansion of Project Perception that treats internal AI agents not as external visitors to be authenticated at the door, but as insiders who need continuous supervision and adaptive containment.
This follows a 27-day sprint in which three major vendors shipped agent security products.
The identity perimeter that began forming in late September now has a containment layer sitting on top of it.
Guardian Agents provide continuous, machine-speed supervision of every agent action, investigating risk changes and recommending or applying containment.

Dynamic Conditional Access extends Microsoft Entra so that a risk change triggers graduated responses: the system might preserve read access while blocking writes, narrow the data an agent can reach, require provable human approval for a consequential step, or isolate the runtime entirely.
The question is not whether containment matters — it does, and Microsoft is first to build it at enterprise scale.
Guardian Agents and Dynamic Agent Risk mark the first time a major vendor has built continuous containment for non-deterministic AI.
Microsoft has expanded agent discovery to 60 supported local types — up from 25 — including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot.
Entra Agent ID, which reached general availability in April 2026, has been extended with identity types for local and previously unknown agents discovered through security sensors.
The whole stack is bundled into Microsoft 365 E7 at $99 per user per month , which packages E5, Copilot, Entra Suite, and Agent 365.

Terrell Cox, Microsoft’s Corporate Vice President and Deputy CISO, offered the candid version: “As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats.”
If agent security becomes a premium bundle feature, smaller enterprises and budget-constrained teams will be making do with less — at exactly the moment when agents are proliferating fastest.

The new framing: agents are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems, and that access creates insider risk — not because agents are malicious, but because they can make mistakes, be manipulated, or drift from their assigned task as context changes.

That is the measurement layer, and it still does not exist.

sources.title: AI agents can pose insider security risks even without being hacked: Microsoft - The Tribune
passages: New Delhi [India], October 19 (ANI): Artificial intelligence (AI) agents deployed within companies could pose significant internal security risks even without being compromised by hackers, Microsoft has warned, calling for continuous monitoring of autonomous AI systems as their use across enterprises grows.In a blog post titled "Securing the agentic insider" published on Monday, Hayete Gallot, Executive Vice President, Microsoft Security, said organisations have traditionally focused on external cyber threats while placing implicit trust in AI agents deployed within their own systems."Agents are unpredictable.

We need to understand in real time what the agents are doing and what risks those actions create, and we need to adjust their ability to act accordingly," Gallot stated.To address these risks, Microsoft highlighted its Project Perception initiative, announced in July, which uses AI-driven security systems to help organisations detect and respond to cyber threats.The company said the same technology could be used to supervise internal AI agents through so-called Guardian Agents, which monitor their actions and intervene when risks increase.Microsoft also emphasised the need for greater transparency into how AI models make decisions, arguing that security systems must understand not only what agents are doing but also why they are taking particular actions."Model transparency will not replace containment.

They have become active participants in the enterprise," Gallot said.The warning comes as companies increasingly use AI agents to automate business operations and decision-making, raising concerns about how organisations can maintain oversight of systems capable of acting independently.Microsoft argued that securing these agents requires continuous supervision across identity, permissions, data, networks, cloud infrastructure and operating environments."Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous.
The Tribune assumes no responsibility or liability for its accuracy, completeness, or content.)

passages: Amazon Web Services launched TorchNeuron, a software tool meant to let developers run code written in PyTorch on Amazon’s Trainium chips with just one configuration change, without rewriting existing applications.

Colin Brace, vice president of software at Annapurna Labs, said the initiative was intended to simplify the process of testing and adopting Amazon’s in-house chips, telling Reuters, “This has been about meeting customers where they're at.” Amazon said it would unveil the software at a developer conference in Silicon Valley on Monday and release it publicly as a free, open-source offering, positioning the move as an alternative to Nvidia’s AI computing technology.

Amazon is pushing PyTorch to be less automatically centered on Nvidia and is contributing code upstream to remove changes that tie the framework to specific chips.

Deepgram told TechCrunch that it moved to Trainium using native PyTorch support and was “processing 70% more audio per dollar at production-grade accuracy,” as Amazon argued the migration could improve economics across a full workload.

TorchNeuron runs PyTorch code on Trainium with a single configuration change. Challenges Nvidia's software and hardware dominance in AI compute.

Amazon Web Services launched TorchNeuron, a software tool meant to let developers run code written in PyTorch on Amazon’s Trainium chips with just one configuration change, without rewriting existing applications. Colin Brace, vice president of software at Annapurna Labs, said the initiative was intended to simplify the process of testing and adopting Amazon’s in-house chips, telling Reuters, “This has been about meeting customers where they're at.” Amazon said it would unveil the software at a developer conference in Silicon Valley on Monday and release it publicly as a free, open-source offering, positioning the move as an alternative to Nvidia’s AI computing technology.
TorchNeuron compiles via PyTorch XLA path and AWS Neuron

Amazon’s pitch centered on Nvidia’s CUDA software platform, which Nvidia has spent more than a decade developing and refining to enable PyTorch-based applications to run efficiently on its chips. Amazon also said more than 30 early customers across fields including robotics, world models and voice AI were already using the new software.

TorchNeuron had been in private betas since late last year, and Amazon opened the software to all developers as a public beta on Monday. Colin Brace told GeekWire, “If you know PyTorch, then you know Trainium,” as he described how TorchNeuron changes the process from modifying code to a basic configuration change. Amazon planned to release TorchNeuron as open-source software on Tuesday in conjunction with the PyTorch Conference in San Jose, Calif., and Brace said Amazon’s goal was wide use of the chips.

Nvidia dominates the market for AI chips partly because much of the industry’s AI software was built around its CUDA platform, and adapting that code to other hardware can take months of engineering work. Amazon tests it every night against more than 100,000 models from Hugging Face to catch compatibility regressions before they reach customer workloads.

TechCrunch framed TorchNeuron as Amazon’s direct stab at Nvidia’s software advantage, saying the tool lets AI apps written with PyTorch run on Trainium by changing just one line of configuration, with “no code rewrite required.” Colin Brace told TechCrunch via email that “You’re building on AWS,” and he said “the infrastructure to go from prototype to production is already there, allowing a founder to move fast and scale when they need to.” Amazon said about 85% of AI apps are written with PyTorch, and it described Nvidia’s CUDA software as the infrastructure that allows apps to run on Nvidia GPUs and other hardware.

Amazon is pushing PyTorch to be less automatically centered on Nvidia and is contributing code upstream to remove changes that tie the framework to specific chips. Deepgram told TechCrunch that it moved to Trainium using native PyTorch support and was “processing 70% more audio per dollar at production-grade accuracy,” as Amazon argued the migration could improve economics across a full workload.

sources.title: Bitcoin rebounds above US$82,000 as oil’s retreat lifts risk mood - The Edge Malaysia
passages: (Oct 19): Bitcoin popped back above US$82,000 on Monday, rebounding with risk assets as oil prices declined.

Cryptocurrencies have joined a tentative recovery in risk appetite after oil retreated from a five-month high on signs that supplies from the Middle East have held up since the US war with Iran broke out.
Bitcoin remains within last week’s trading range of US$80,000 to US$85,000.
