extraction.body: By Pratik Ghadge Wednesday September 30, 2026 DeepSeek and Huawei are working together on a new set of open-source programming tools for Huawei’s Ascend artificial intelligence chips, tackling one of the biggest challenges facing any company trying to compete with Nvidia: software. The Chinese AI developer has released infrastructure for Huawei’s Ascend platform that includes TileLang , a high-level programming language, alongside compute and communication libraries designed to make it easier for developers to use Ascend hardware. The project is important because Nvidia’s advantage in artificial intelligence has never depended on chips alone. CUDA, its long-established software platform, gives developers a mature collection of tools for building and optimising applications around Nvidia GPUs. DeepSeek and Huawei are now trying to make the software experience around Ascend chips considerably easier. Programming high-performance AI hardware usually requires developers to balance two competing goals. TileLang is only one component of the open-source effort. DeepSeek is also releasing related compute and distributed-communication libraries for Huawei’s Ascend platform. Compute libraries provide optimised building blocks for operations that AI models repeatedly perform, while communication libraries help large groups of processors exchange data efficiently. Training or serving a large model may require hundreds or thousands of accelerators operating together. The speed of individual chips matters, but so does the efficiency with which they communicate across the wider computing system. The DeepSeek Huawei partnership is therefore working on the broader software infrastructure rather than treating TileLang as a standalone project. Open sourcing the tools could help the platform gain users more quickly. Developers can inspect the software, experiment with it and contribute improvements rather than waiting entirely for one company to add every feature. That approach has already played an important role in DeepSeek’s rise. The company has released major AI models and supporting technologies openly, allowing developers around the world to test, modify and deploy them. Applying a similar strategy to AI-chip software could help Huawei attract more development activity around Ascend. The immediate challenge will be making sure the open-source tools are mature enough for production workloads. CUDA has had years to develop, so catching up will require much more than one software release. Huawei has been expanding the Ascend family as demand for computing power used by AI models continues to rise. DeepSeek has already been working closely with that hardware. Earlier in 2026, Huawei said its Ascend supernode infrastructure would support DeepSeek’s V4 models . More recently, DeepSeek has been linked with plans to deploy a very large number of Huawei accelerators in new computing infrastructure. The new Ascend AI software makes that hardware relationship more practical for developers as well. A faster processor offers limited value if engineering teams have to spend months rewriting software to make it work. This is where Nvidia’s mature ecosystem has historically been particularly difficult to challenge. DeepSeek says TileLang offers a simpler programming model than CUDA, but that claim does not mean the new platform already matches CUDA’s overall ecosystem. CUDA includes a much wider collection of tools, libraries and software accumulated over many years. TileLang should therefore be viewed as one part of an effort to reduce the programming gap rather than a complete replacement appearing overnight. DeepSeek brings something particularly valuable to the partnership: experience building and operating large AI models. A chip company can design software tools internally, but feedback from a major model developer can help expose what programmers actually need when handling demanding AI workloads. DeepSeek says operators used in its own training environment now have high-performance implementations for Ascend. It represents an attempt to build the software layer needed around an alternative AI-computing ecosystem. Nvidia has demonstrated that great chips and great software reinforce one another. Huawei has been building the hardware. DeepSeek’s latest move shows the next battle may increasingly be about making that hardware just as straightforward for developers to program. Chinese AI giant DeepSeek has apparently encountered unexpected delays in releasing its latest model, R2, after facing persistent technical difficulties with Huawei’s Ascend chips. The company had been encouraged by Chinese authorities to adopt domestic processors instead of relying on Nvidia’s H20 systems , which are generally regarded as more mature and reliable. Despite Huawei engineers being on-site to assist, DeepSeek could not complete a successful training run using Ascend chips - and as a result, the company relied on Nvidia hardware for training while using Ascend for inference tasks. The R2 launch, originally scheduled for May 2025, was postponed due to these technical obstacles and longer-than-expected data labeling for the updated training dataset. DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng reportedly expressed dissatisfaction with the model’s progress, emphasizing the need for additional development time to produce a model capable of maintaining DeepSeek’s competitive edge. Meanwhile, competitors like Alibaba’s Qwen3 were able to take advantage of this delay, as it has incorporated DeepSeek’s core training algorithms while improving efficiency and flexibility, showing how rapidly AI ecosystems can evolve even when a single startup struggles. Beijing’s broader push for AI self-sufficiency has placed pressure on domestic firms to adopt local hardware. In practice, however, this strategy has revealed gaps in stability, inter-chip connectivity, and software maturity between Huawei chips and Nvidia products. Developers continue to play a crucial role in shaping the success of AI ecosystems - Nvidia has emphasized maintaining access to Chinese developers is strategically important, warning that restricting technology adoption could harm economic and national security interests. Chinese AI companies, meanwhile, must balance government pressures with practical realities in developing and deploying LLMs . Despite these setbacks, DeepSeek’s R2 model may still be released in the coming weeks. The model is likely to face scrutiny regarding its performance relative to rivals trained on more mature hardware, offering a clear example of the tension between political ambitions, technical capability, and real-world AI deployment. The DeepSeek AI chip project focuses on inference, the stage of AI computing where a trained model produces answers for users in real time. This is distinct from training, which involves building a model from scratch using massive datasets and thousands of GPUs over weeks or months. Reuters reports that the effort began about a year ago. DeepSeek has held discussions with chip-design firms, foundries, and memory suppliers, and has been quietly expanding its semiconductor engineering team. Recruitment has been handled privately, without public job postings, according to two of the three sources. The project remains at an early stage. No foundry, process node, or timeline to first silicon has been disclosed, and DeepSeek has not commented publicly on the report. Inference is different in three important ways: This may explain why DeepSeek is not attempting to replace NVIDIA’s training dominance. Instead, it is attacking the segment where a homegrown chip could deliver the fastest return and face the least resistance from export controls. DeepSeek is joining a global wave of AI companies building proprietary silicon to reduce dependence on NVIDIA. The list now includes most of the industry’s largest spenders. OpenAI unveiled Jalapeño , its first custom inference chip, on June 24. Built in partnership with Broadcom in just nine months, the chip is designed for LLM inference and targets deployment by late 2026. Anthropic has also been weighing its own chip program, according to a separate Reuters report from April 2026. Beyond the frontier labs, hyperscalers have been investing in custom AI silicon for years. Google runs its Tensor Processing Units across most internal AI workloads. Amazon is now exploring direct sales of its Trainium processors to third-party data centers. Microsoft launched the Maia 200 accelerator in early 2026, which already powers GPT-5.2 models on Azure. The Chinese AI developer has released infrastructure for Huawei’s Ascend platform that includes TileLang , a high-level programming language, alongside compute and communication libraries designed to make it easier for developers to use Ascend hardware. The project is important because Nvidia’s advantage in artificial intelligence has never depended on chips alone. CUDA, its long-established software platform, gives developers a mature collection of tools for building and optimising applications around Nvidia GPUs. DeepSeek and Huawei are now trying to make the software experience around Ascend chips considerably easier. Programming high-performance AI hardware usually requires developers to balance two competing goals. TileLang is only one component of the open-source effort. DeepSeek is also releasing related compute and distributed-communication libraries for Huawei’s Ascend platform. Compute libraries provide optimised building blocks for operations that AI models repeatedly perform, while communication libraries help large groups of processors exchange data efficiently. Training or serving a large model may require hundreds or thousands of accelerators operating together. The speed of individual chips matters, but so does the efficiency with which they communicate across the wider computing system. The DeepSeek Huawei partnership is therefore working on the broader software infrastructure rather than treating TileLang as a standalone project. Open sourcing the tools could help the platform gain users more quickly. Developers can inspect the software, experiment with it and contribute improvements rather than waiting entirely for one company to add every feature. That approach has already played an important role in DeepSeek’s rise. The company has released major AI models and supporting technologies openly, allowing developers around the world to test, modify and deploy them. Applying a similar strategy to AI-chip software could help Huawei attract more development activity around Ascend. The immediate challenge will be making sure the open-source tools are mature enough for production workloads. CUDA has had years to develop, so catching up will require much more than one software release. Huawei has been expanding the Ascend family as demand for computing power used by AI models continues to rise. DeepSeek has already been working closely with that hardware. Earlier in 2026, Huawei said its Ascend supernode infrastructure would support DeepSeek’s V4 models . More recently, DeepSeek has been linked with plans to deploy a very large number of Huawei accelerators in new computing infrastructure. The new Ascend AI software makes that hardware relationship more practical for developers as well. A faster processor offers limited value if engineering teams have to spend months rewriting software to make it work. This is where Nvidia’s mature ecosystem has historically been particularly difficult to challenge. DeepSeek says TileLang offers a simpler programming model than CUDA, but that claim does not mean the new platform already matches CUDA’s overall ecosystem. CUDA includes a much wider collection of tools, libraries and software accumulated over many years. TileLang should therefore be viewed as one part of an effort to reduce the programming gap rather than a complete replacement appearing overnight. DeepSeek brings something particularly valuable to the partnership: experience building and operating large AI models. A chip company can design software tools internally, but feedback from a major model developer can help expose what programmers actually need when handling demanding AI workloads. DeepSeek says operators used in its own training environment now have high-performance implementations for Ascend. It represents an attempt to build the software layer needed around an alternative AI-computing ecosystem. Nvidia has demonstrated that great chips and great software reinforce one another. Huawei has been building the hardware. DeepSeek’s latest move shows the next battle may increasingly be about making that hardware just as straightforward for developers to program. passages: We introduced Project Perception and the Microsoft cyber stack to help organizations defend with agents.
Today, we are extending Perception to secure the agentic insider .

Guardian Agents help security teams operate continuously, at machine speed and scale, while sensors, context, and actuators across the cyber stack help understand changing agent risk and continuously adapt protection in response.
Agents can be created through Microsoft platforms, integrated through partner platforms and software development kits (SDKs), or introduced locally without a central deployment process.
An agent should not be free to call any tool, API, Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, resource, or other agent it can find.
Local and network and data controls must mediate those paths, observe the calls, and enforce enterprise policy.
Controlling the destination alone is not enough.
Security must also understand the content flowing into and out of the agent, including its sensitivity, provenance, and whether untrusted data may be influencing the agent’s behavior.
Agents are rapidly becoming part of how work gets done.
They can support a range of activities from writing code and researching products to analyzing revenue, processing expenses, and acting across the systems that run the business.
To be most useful, they often need access to company data, applications, tools, and other agents.
That access is what makes agents more capable.

Satya Nadella, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Microsoft, recently described the trust architecture this new era requires: we must separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.
We should not ask a model to be its own security authority.
The controls that determine what it can access, what actions it can take, and whether it should continue operating must sit outside the model, where the model cannot bypass or tamper with them.

Sandboxes such as Microsoft Execution Container (MXC) provide policy-controlled access to resources the agent needs to complete its task.
Agents will only be adopted at scale if they can be trusted at scale.
At Microsoft, we are already operating in a world of hundreds of thousands of agents.

extraction.body: Agents are rapidly becoming part of how work gets done. They can support a range of activities from writing code and researching products to analyzing revenue, processing expenses, and acting across the systems that run the business. To be most useful, they often need access to company data, applications, tools, and other agents. That access is what makes agents more capable. With that capability can come insider risk. This does not mean agents are inherently malicious. It means they are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems by users. They can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised. Their models can produce variable outputs, their context can change, and their plans can evolve as they work. An agent that operates as intended when a task begins may respond differently as context or inputs change. Depending on how they are designed and deployed, agents can operate continuously, at machine speed and scale. Satya Nadella, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Microsoft, recently described the trust architecture this new era requires: we must separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. We should not ask a model to be its own security authority. The controls that determine what it can access, what actions it can take, and whether it should continue operating must sit outside the model, where the model cannot bypass or tamper with them. “The most trustworthy agentic system will not be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one designed that enables us to trust the model least.” We introduced Project Perception and the Microsoft cyber stack to help organizations defend with agents. Today, we are extending Perception to secure the agentic insider . Guardian Agents help security teams operate continuously, at machine speed and scale, while sensors, context, and actuators across the cyber stack help understand changing agent risk and continuously adapt protection in response. Project Perception and Microsoft Agent 365 share signals, context, and a unified registry giving IT and security teams a consistent view of agents and risk, with the controls each needs. This builds on a simple security principle: surround non-deterministic intelligence with deterministic controls, independent evidence, and containment boundaries. Assume an agent can fail or be compromised. Observe it continuously. Minimize and tailor its authority before it acts. And continuously adjust that authority as risk changes. This requires protection across identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud, and runtime. The system has four continuous responsibilities: These are not four products or sequential phases. They operate together. Evidence changes risk. Risk changes policy. Policy changes what the agent is allowed to do. Consider an expense-approval agent. It may need to read expense submissions, check policy, and approve routine reimbursements, but it should not inherit every permission of the employee who sponsors it. Its identity, runtime, access paths, and task-scoped authority should be explicit from the start. If it later encounters a prompt injection or attempts an action outside that task, the system should respond proportionately: preserve safe reads while blocking writes, narrow the resources it can reach, require provable human approval for a consequential step, or isolate and stop the agent when the risk warrants it. This is what continuous containment looks like in practice. You cannot secure what you cannot see. Agents can be created through Microsoft platforms, integrated through partner platforms and software development kits (SDKs), or introduced locally without a central deployment process. Microsoft Security uses native integrations, connectors, and sensors across the cyber stack to discover more of the agent estate. We are expanding discovery to 35 additional types of local agents, bringing the total to 60 supported local agents , including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot. Organizations can bring these agents into a unified registry, regardless of how they were discovered, to understand ownership, activity, and risk. Discovery tells you that an agent exists. Identity gives security and governance systems a durable anchor for controlling it. Every agent should have a first-class identity distinct from the person using or sponsoring it. We are extending Microsoft Entra Agent ID with identity types for additional agent patterns, including local and previously unknown agents discovered through security sensors. This means an agent can become a policy target even when it was not originally integrated with Microsoft Security. Agent identity anchors attribution, ownership, lifecycle, risk, permissions, authorization, and policy, so the enterprise can distinguish what a person did from what an agent did on that person’s behalf. Being able to find and identify an agent is necessary, but it is just the start. We need to understand the potential impact the agent can have in the enterprise environment. The next step is to bound the agent across its runtime, its paths to tools and resources, and the authority it can exercise. The model and harness should execute inside a controlled environment rather than inherit fully-privileged access to the device. Sandboxes such as Microsoft Execution Container (MXC) provide policy-controlled access to resources the agent needs to complete its task. They also create an enforcement boundary where security controls and observability can operate outside the agent’s reach. If the agent or harness is compromised, it should not be able to disable the controls watching it. An agent should not be free to call any tool, API, Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, resource, or other agent it can find. Local and network and data controls must mediate those paths, observe the calls, and enforce enterprise policy. Controlling the destination alone is not enough. Security must also understand the content flowing into and out of the agent, including its sensitivity, provenance, and whether untrusted data may be influencing the agent’s behavior. We have spent decades applying Zero Trust and least privilege to people. Agents make those principles even more important. An agent should not automatically inherit all the standing access of its user. It should begin with no authority and receive only what it needs for the approved task, for only as long as the task requires. Least privilege reduces exposure, but it does not eliminate risk. An expense-approval agent may begin a task with the right access and then encounter a prompt injection in an external document. Its configuration has not changed, but its behavior and risk have. For human users, a delay between detection and response may be manageable. For an agent operating at machine speed, it can be the difference between containment and impact. The security system must be able to understand what changed and act before a person can manually investigate every signal. That is why we are introducing Dynamic Agent Risk and Dynamic Conditional Access for agents. The result is not a one-time score assigned at onboarding. It is a continuously updated understanding of the agent’s current risk and whether its current authority still matches that risk. The question is not simply whether the agent should run or stop. It is what the agent should be allowed to read, change, invoke, or approve at that moment. Dynamic Conditional Access extends Microsoft Entra Conditional Access for agents so a change in risk can drive coordinated action across multiple enforcement points. The response is graduated, not binary. Policy can reduce permissions, preserve reads while blocking writes, narrow the data and resources the agent can reach, restrict network paths, shorten or revoke time-bound access, or require provable human approval before a consequential action proceeds. At the highest levels of risk, it can isolate the runtime or stop execution entirely. Return to the expense agent. It begins with narrowly scoped permission to review and approve expenses within policy. When it encounters untrusted content and attempts an unrelated action, new evidence raises its Dynamic Agent Risk. Policy responds proportionately: it can preserve read access while removing the ability to approve or write, block access to sensitive resources, and require cryptographically provable human approval for a high-impact step. If the risk continues to rise, the system can isolate the runtime or stop execution. The employee remains productive. The agent is constrained without treating every risk change as a kill-switch event. As organizations deploy thousands or hundreds of thousands of agents, manually triaging every alert and coordinating every response will not scale. Securing agents must itself become agentic, while remaining inside boundaries people set. That is why we are introducing new Playbooks and a team of Guardian Agents in Project Perception. People define policy, approval boundaries, and delegation rules. Playbooks define the desired security outcome and coordinate protective actions. Guardian Agents carry out the work at machine speed, adapting as agent activity, risk, security context, and organizational policy change. Guardian Agents can help teams understand why risk changed, investigate the relevant evidence, recommend or apply containment, and use what they learn to harden policy. This is not about outsourcing judgment. People retain control over objectives and consequential decisions. The system carries the continuous work that does not scale through manual operations. Agents will only be adopted at scale if they can be trusted at scale. At Microsoft, we are already operating in a world of hundreds of thousands of agents. As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats. Those lessons directly inform the innovations we are delivering to help every organization adopt agents with confidence.” — Terrell Cox, Corporate Vice President (CVP) and Deputy Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), Customer Security, Microsoft As model transparency increases, it creates a new source of security evidence. Chain-of-thought and other model-level signals can help identify intent drift, understand whether untrusted information is influencing reasoning, and detect when an agent’s planned actions are diverging from the task it was given. We are bringing this deeper evidence into Dynamic Agent Risk, together with signals from across the cyber stack. This builds on Satya Nadella’s principle: increase transparency into the model while keeping security decisions and enforcement independent of it. Greater model transparency gives security systems deeper evidence to detect suspicious behavior and inform Dynamic Agent Risk. But the core security principle does not change: the model cannot be its own security boundary. Independent systems must observe every layer, including the model itself, and ultimately determine and enforce what the system is allowed to do. These are not separate pillars. They make the same containment architecture stronger: better evidence, stronger assurance, more accurate risk, and more effective protection. Organizations are adopting agents to serve customers better, solve problems faster, and give people more time for the work that matters most. The goal is not to make every model perfectly predictable before it can be useful. The goal is to build systems that remain secure even when the model is not. That requires a clear division of responsibility. Models supply intelligence. People and organizations retain authority. Independent controls establish identity, limit privilege, protect data, preserve evidence, and contain unsafe action. Security continuously reassesses risk and adapts protection as the agent works. You should not have to choose between innovation and safety. Corporate Vice President, Identity and Network Access, Microsoft Protect your people, data, and infrastructure with AI-powered, end-to-end security from Microsoft.

This requires protection across identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud, and runtime. The system has four continuous responsibilities:

These are not four products or sequential phases. They operate together. Evidence changes risk. Risk changes policy. Policy changes what the agent is allowed to do. Consider an expense-approval agent. It may need to read expense submissions, check policy, and approve routine reimbursements, but it should not inherit every permission of the employee who sponsors it. Its identity, runtime, access paths, and task-scoped authority should be explicit from the start. If it later encounters a prompt injection or attempts an action outside that task, the system should respond proportionately: preserve safe reads while blocking writes, narrow the resources it can reach, require provable human approval for a consequential step, or isolate and stop the agent when the risk warrants it. This is what continuous containment looks like in practice.

You cannot secure what you cannot see. Agents can be created through Microsoft platforms, integrated through partner platforms and software development kits (SDKs), or introduced locally without a central deployment process. Microsoft Security uses native integrations, connectors, and sensors across the cyber stack to discover more of the agent estate.

We are expanding discovery to 35 additional types of local agents, bringing the total to 60 supported local agents , including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot. Organizations can bring these agents into a unified registry, regardless of how they were discovered, to understand ownership, activity, and risk.
Discovery tells you that an agent exists. Identity gives security and governance systems a durable anchor for controlling it.

Every agent should have a first-class identity distinct from the person using or sponsoring it. We are extending Microsoft Entra Agent ID with identity types for additional agent patterns, including local and previously unknown agents discovered through security sensors. This means an agent can become a policy target even when it was not originally integrated with Microsoft Security. Agent identity anchors attribution, ownership, lifecycle, risk, permissions, authorization, and policy, so the enterprise can distinguish what a person did from what an agent did on that person’s behalf.

Being able to find and identify an agent is necessary, but it is just the start. We need to understand the potential impact the agent can have in the enterprise environment. The next step is to bound the agent across its runtime, its paths to tools and resources, and the authority it can exercise.

The model and harness should execute inside a controlled environment rather than inherit fully-privileged access to the device. Sandboxes such as Microsoft Execution Container (MXC) provide policy-controlled access to resources the agent needs to complete its task. They also create an enforcement boundary where security controls and observability can operate outside the agent’s reach. If the agent or harness is compromised, it should not be able to disable the controls watching it.

An agent should not be free to call any tool, API, Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, resource, or other agent it can find. Local and network and data controls must mediate those paths, observe the calls, and enforce enterprise policy. Controlling the destination alone is not enough. Security must also understand the content flowing into and out of the agent, including its sensitivity, provenance, and whether untrusted data may be influencing the agent’s behavior.

We have spent decades applying Zero Trust and least privilege to people. Agents make those principles even more important. An agent should not automatically inherit all the standing access of its user. It should begin with no authority and receive only what it needs for the approved task, for only as long as the task requires.

Least privilege reduces exposure, but it does not eliminate risk. An expense-approval agent may begin a task with the right access and then encounter a prompt injection in an external document. Its configuration has not changed, but its behavior and risk have.

For human users, a delay between detection and response may be manageable. For an agent operating at machine speed, it can be the difference between containment and impact. The security system must be able to understand what changed and act before a person can manually investigate every signal.
That is why we are introducing Dynamic Agent Risk and Dynamic Conditional Access for agents.

The result is not a one-time score assigned at onboarding. It is a continuously updated understanding of the agent’s current risk and whether its current authority still matches that risk. The question is not simply whether the agent should run or stop. It is what the agent should be allowed to read, change, invoke, or approve at that moment.

Dynamic Conditional Access extends Microsoft Entra Conditional Access for agents so a change in risk can drive coordinated action across multiple enforcement points. The response is graduated, not binary. Policy can reduce permissions, preserve reads while blocking writes, narrow the data and resources the agent can reach, restrict network paths, shorten or revoke time-bound access, or require provable human approval before a consequential action proceeds. At the highest levels of risk, it can isolate the runtime or stop execution entirely.

Return to the expense agent. It begins with narrowly scoped permission to review and approve expenses within policy. When it encounters untrusted content and attempts an unrelated action, new evidence raises its Dynamic Agent Risk. Policy responds proportionately: it can preserve read access while removing the ability to approve or write, block access to sensitive resources, and require cryptographically provable human approval for a high-impact step. If the risk continues to rise, the system can isolate the runtime or stop execution. The employee remains productive. The agent is constrained without treating every risk change as a kill-switch event.

As organizations deploy thousands or hundreds of thousands of agents, manually triaging every alert and coordinating every response will not scale. Securing agents must itself become agentic, while remaining inside boundaries people set.

That is why we are introducing new Playbooks and a team of Guardian Agents in Project Perception. People define policy, approval boundaries, and delegation rules. Playbooks define the desired security outcome and coordinate protective actions. Guardian Agents carry out the work at machine speed, adapting as agent activity, risk, security context, and organizational policy change.

Guardian Agents can help teams understand why risk changed, investigate the relevant evidence, recommend or apply containment, and use what they learn to harden policy. This is not about outsourcing judgment. People retain control over objectives and consequential decisions. The system carries the continuous work that does not scale through manual operations.

Agents will only be adopted at scale if they can be trusted at scale. At Microsoft, we are already operating in a world of hundreds of thousands of agents. As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats. Those lessons directly inform the innovations we are delivering to help every organization adopt agents with confidence.”
— Terrell Cox, Corporate Vice President (CVP) and Deputy Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), Customer Security, Microsoft

As model transparency increases, it creates a new source of security evidence. Chain-of-thought and other model-level signals can help identify intent drift, understand whether untrusted information is influencing reasoning, and detect when an agent’s planned actions are diverging from the task it was given.

We are bringing this deeper evidence into Dynamic Agent Risk, together with signals from across the cyber stack. This builds on Satya Nadella’s principle: increase transparency into the model while keeping security decisions and enforcement independent of it.

Greater model transparency gives security systems deeper evidence to detect suspicious behavior and inform Dynamic Agent Risk. But the core security principle does not change: the model cannot be its own security boundary. Independent systems must observe every layer, including the model itself, and ultimately determine and enforce what the system is allowed to do.
These are not separate pillars. They make the same containment architecture stronger: better evidence, stronger assurance, more accurate risk, and more effective protection.

Organizations are adopting agents to serve customers better, solve problems faster, and give people more time for the work that matters most. The goal is not to make every model perfectly predictable before it can be useful. The goal is to build systems that remain secure even when the model is not.

That requires a clear division of responsibility. Models supply intelligence. People and organizations retain authority. Independent controls establish identity, limit privilege, protect data, preserve evidence, and contain unsafe action. Security continuously reassesses risk and adapts protection as the agent works.
You should not have to choose between innovation and safety.
Corporate Vice President, Identity and Network Access, Microsoft
Protect your people, data, and infrastructure with AI-powered, end-to-end security from Microsoft.

sources.title: Microsoft Treats AI Agents as Insiders — and the Containment Layer Just Arrived - Forkast News
passages: Microsoft just moved the goalposts on what it means to secure an AI agent.

On October 19, the company announced an expansion of Project Perception that treats internal AI agents not as external visitors to be authenticated at the door, but as insiders who need continuous supervision and adaptive containment.
This follows a 27-day sprint in which three major vendors shipped agent security products.
The identity perimeter that began forming in late September now has a containment layer sitting on top of it.
Guardian Agents provide continuous, machine-speed supervision of every agent action, investigating risk changes and recommending or applying containment.

Dynamic Conditional Access extends Microsoft Entra so that a risk change triggers graduated responses: the system might preserve read access while blocking writes, narrow the data an agent can reach, require provable human approval for a consequential step, or isolate the runtime entirely.
The question is not whether containment matters — it does, and Microsoft is first to build it at enterprise scale.
Guardian Agents and Dynamic Agent Risk mark the first time a major vendor has built continuous containment for non-deterministic AI.
Microsoft has expanded agent discovery to 60 supported local types — up from 25 — including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot.
Entra Agent ID, which reached general availability in April 2026, has been extended with identity types for local and previously unknown agents discovered through security sensors.
The whole stack is bundled into Microsoft 365 E7 at $99 per user per month , which packages E5, Copilot, Entra Suite, and Agent 365.

Terrell Cox, Microsoft’s Corporate Vice President and Deputy CISO, offered the candid version: “As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats.”
If agent security becomes a premium bundle feature, smaller enterprises and budget-constrained teams will be making do with less — at exactly the moment when agents are proliferating fastest.

The new framing: agents are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems, and that access creates insider risk — not because agents are malicious, but because they can make mistakes, be manipulated, or drift from their assigned task as context changes.

The new framing: agents are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems, and that access creates insider risk — not because agents are malicious, but because they can make mistakes, be manipulated, or drift from their assigned task as context changes.

The product details are specific. Guardian Agents provide continuous, machine-speed supervision of every agent action, investigating risk changes and recommending or applying containment. Dynamic Agent Risk calculates a continuously updated risk score by combining signals from identity, data, endpoints, cloud, network, runtime, and the agent’s own activity — including chain-of-thought analysis for intent drift. And Dynamic Permissions ensures agents start with zero authority and receive only task-scoped, time-bound access.

Satya Nadella framed the principle plainly: “The most trustworthy agentic system will not be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one designed that enables us to trust the model least.”

Microsoft has expanded agent discovery to 60 supported local types — up from 25 — including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot. Entra Agent ID, which reached general availability in April 2026, has been extended with identity types for local and previously unknown agents discovered through security sensors. The whole stack is bundled into Microsoft 365 E7 at $99 per user per month , which packages E5, Copilot, Entra Suite, and Agent 365.

This follows a 27-day sprint in which three major vendors shipped agent security products. Okta launched Agent SSO on September 22. ServiceNow introduced AI Passport on October 15. Microsoft followed on October 19. The identity perimeter that began forming in late September now has a containment layer sitting on top of it.

But the measurement gap has not closed. The Okta AI Agents at Work 2026 survey found 96% of executives confident in their identity and access management for non-human identities, yet only 34% actually apply the same controls they use for human employees. The Saviynt CISO AI Risk Report 2026 found 92% of CISOs lack full visibility into AI agent identities. And the NIST AI Risk Management Framework MEASURE function — the part that would tell you whether an agent’s actions align with its intended purpose — scored 0.6 out of 5.0, rated critical.

Terrell Cox, Microsoft’s Corporate Vice President and Deputy CISO, offered the candid version: “As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats.”

The question is not whether containment matters — it does, and Microsoft is first to build it at enterprise scale. The question is what containment cannot tell you. Dynamic Agent Risk can stop an agent from doing damage. It can narrow permissions in real time, require human approval, or kill the runtime. What it cannot yet tell you is whether the agent is actually doing its job correctly — whether the expense it approved was the right call, whether the code it wrote matches the spec, whether the research it produced is accurate. That is the measurement layer, and it still does not exist.

The $99 per user per month price tag also raises a practical question about who gets access to this kind of containment. If agent security becomes a premium bundle feature, smaller enterprises and budget-constrained teams will be making do with less — at exactly the moment when agents are proliferating fastest.

passages: New Delhi [India], October 19 (ANI): Artificial intelligence (AI) agents deployed within companies could pose significant internal security risks even without being compromised by hackers, Microsoft has warned, calling for continuous monitoring of autonomous AI systems as their use across enterprises grows.In a blog post titled "Securing the agentic insider" published on Monday, Hayete Gallot, Executive Vice President, Microsoft Security, said organisations have traditionally focused on external cyber threats while placing implicit trust in AI agents deployed within their own systems."Agents are unpredictable.

We need to understand in real time what the agents are doing and what risks those actions create, and we need to adjust their ability to act accordingly," Gallot stated.To address these risks, Microsoft highlighted its Project Perception initiative, announced in July, which uses AI-driven security systems to help organisations detect and respond to cyber threats.The company said the same technology could be used to supervise internal AI agents through so-called Guardian Agents, which monitor their actions and intervene when risks increase.Microsoft also emphasised the need for greater transparency into how AI models make decisions, arguing that security systems must understand not only what agents are doing but also why they are taking particular actions."Model transparency will not replace containment.

They have become active participants in the enterprise," Gallot said.The warning comes as companies increasingly use AI agents to automate business operations and decision-making, raising concerns about how organisations can maintain oversight of systems capable of acting independently.Microsoft argued that securing these agents requires continuous supervision across identity, permissions, data, networks, cloud infrastructure and operating environments."Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous.
The Tribune assumes no responsibility or liability for its accuracy, completeness, or content.)

relevantPassages.text: New Delhi [India], October 19 (ANI): Artificial intelligence (AI) agents deployed within companies could pose significant internal security risks even without being compromised by hackers, Microsoft has warned, calling for continuous monitoring of autonomous AI systems as their use across enterprises grows.In a blog post titled "Securing the agentic insider" published on Monday, Hayete Gallot, Executive Vice President, Microsoft Security, said organisations have traditionally focused on external cyber threats while placing implicit trust in AI agents deployed within their own systems."Agents are unpredictable.

We need to understand in real time what the agents are doing and what risks those actions create, and we need to adjust their ability to act accordingly," Gallot stated.To address these risks, Microsoft highlighted its Project Perception initiative, announced in July, which uses AI-driven security systems to help organisations detect and respond to cyber threats.The company said the same technology could be used to supervise internal AI agents through so-called Guardian Agents, which monitor their actions and intervene when risks increase.Microsoft also emphasised the need for greater transparency into how AI models make decisions, arguing that security systems must understand not only what agents are doing but also why they are taking particular actions."Model transparency will not replace containment.

They have become active participants in the enterprise," Gallot said.The warning comes as companies increasingly use AI agents to automate business operations and decision-making, raising concerns about how organisations can maintain oversight of systems capable of acting independently.Microsoft argued that securing these agents requires continuous supervision across identity, permissions, data, networks, cloud infrastructure and operating environments."Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous.
The Tribune assumes no responsibility or liability for its accuracy, completeness, or content.)

coreStoryFacts.text: We introduced Project Perception and the Microsoft cyber stack to help organizations defend with agents.
Today, we are extending Perception to secure the agentic insider .

Guardian Agents help security teams operate continuously, at machine speed and scale, while sensors, context, and actuators across the cyber stack help understand changing agent risk and continuously adapt protection in response.
Agents can be created through Microsoft platforms, integrated through partner platforms and software development kits (SDKs), or introduced locally without a central deployment process.
An agent should not be free to call any tool, API, Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, resource, or other agent it can find.
Local and network and data controls must mediate those paths, observe the calls, and enforce enterprise policy.
Controlling the destination alone is not enough.
Security must also understand the content flowing into and out of the agent, including its sensitivity, provenance, and whether untrusted data may be influencing the agent’s behavior.
Agents are rapidly becoming part of how work gets done.
They can support a range of activities from writing code and researching products to analyzing revenue, processing expenses, and acting across the systems that run the business.
To be most useful, they often need access to company data, applications, tools, and other agents.
That access is what makes agents more capable.

Satya Nadella, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Microsoft, recently described the trust architecture this new era requires: we must separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.
We should not ask a model to be its own security authority.
The controls that determine what it can access, what actions it can take, and whether it should continue operating must sit outside the model, where the model cannot bypass or tamper with them.
The security system must be able to understand what changed and act before a person can manually investigate every signal.
This means an agent can become a policy target even when it was not originally integrated with Microsoft Security.
Sandboxes such as Microsoft Execution Container (MXC) provide policy-controlled access to resources the agent needs to complete its task.
Agents will only be adopted at scale if they can be trusted at scale.
At Microsoft, we are already operating in a world of hundreds of thousands of agents.

As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats.
Those lessons directly inform the innovations we are delivering to help every organization adopt agents with confidence.”
— Terrell Cox, Corporate Vice President (CVP) and Deputy Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), Customer Security, Microsoft
That requires a clear division of responsibility.

Independent controls establish identity, limit privilege, protect data, preserve evidence, and contain unsafe action.
Security continuously reassesses risk and adapts protection as the agent works.
Protect your people, data, and infrastructure with AI-powered, end-to-end security from Microsoft.
Greater model transparency gives security systems deeper evidence to detect suspicious behavior and inform Dynamic Agent Risk.
We have spent decades applying Zero Trust and least privilege to people.
Agents make those principles even more important.
Dynamic Conditional Access extends Microsoft Entra Conditional Access for agents so a change in risk can drive coordinated action across multiple enforcement points.
Securing agents must itself become agentic, while remaining inside boundaries people set.

On October 19, the company announced an expansion of Project Perception that treats internal AI agents not as external visitors to be authenticated at the door, but as insiders who need continuous supervision and adaptive containment.
This follows a 27-day sprint in which three major vendors shipped agent security products.
The identity perimeter that began forming in late September now has a containment layer sitting on top of it.
Guardian Agents provide continuous, machine-speed supervision of every agent action, investigating risk changes and recommending or applying containment.

Dynamic Conditional Access extends Microsoft Entra so that a risk change triggers graduated responses: the system might preserve read access while blocking writes, narrow the data an agent can reach, require provable human approval for a consequential step, or isolate the runtime entirely.
The question is not whether containment matters — it does, and Microsoft is first to build it at enterprise scale.
Guardian Agents and Dynamic Agent Risk mark the first time a major vendor has built continuous containment for non-deterministic AI.
Microsoft has expanded agent discovery to 60 supported local types — up from 25 — including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot.
Entra Agent ID, which reached general availability in April 2026, has been extended with identity types for local and previously unknown agents discovered through security sensors.
The whole stack is bundled into Microsoft 365 E7 at $99 per user per month , which packages E5, Copilot, Entra Suite, and Agent 365.

Terrell Cox, Microsoft’s Corporate Vice President and Deputy CISO, offered the candid version: “As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats.”
If agent security becomes a premium bundle feature, smaller enterprises and budget-constrained teams will be making do with less — at exactly the moment when agents are proliferating fastest.

The new framing: agents are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems, and that access creates insider risk — not because agents are malicious, but because they can make mistakes, be manipulated, or drift from their assigned task as context changes.

sources.title: Microsoft Treats AI Agents as Insiders — and the Containment Layer Just Arrived - Forkast News
passages: Microsoft just moved the goalposts on what it means to secure an AI agent.

On October 19, the company announced an expansion of Project Perception that treats internal AI agents not as external visitors to be authenticated at the door, but as insiders who need continuous supervision and adaptive containment.
This follows a 27-day sprint in which three major vendors shipped agent security products.
The identity perimeter that began forming in late September now has a containment layer sitting on top of it.
Guardian Agents provide continuous, machine-speed supervision of every agent action, investigating risk changes and recommending or applying containment.

Dynamic Conditional Access extends Microsoft Entra so that a risk change triggers graduated responses: the system might preserve read access while blocking writes, narrow the data an agent can reach, require provable human approval for a consequential step, or isolate the runtime entirely.
The question is not whether containment matters — it does, and Microsoft is first to build it at enterprise scale.
Guardian Agents and Dynamic Agent Risk mark the first time a major vendor has built continuous containment for non-deterministic AI.
Microsoft has expanded agent discovery to 60 supported local types — up from 25 — including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot.
Entra Agent ID, which reached general availability in April 2026, has been extended with identity types for local and previously unknown agents discovered through security sensors.
The whole stack is bundled into Microsoft 365 E7 at $99 per user per month , which packages E5, Copilot, Entra Suite, and Agent 365.

Terrell Cox, Microsoft’s Corporate Vice President and Deputy CISO, offered the candid version: “As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats.”
If agent security becomes a premium bundle feature, smaller enterprises and budget-constrained teams will be making do with less — at exactly the moment when agents are proliferating fastest.

The new framing: agents are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems, and that access creates insider risk — not because agents are malicious, but because they can make mistakes, be manipulated, or drift from their assigned task as context changes.

On October 19, the company announced an expansion of Project Perception that treats internal AI agents not as external visitors to be authenticated at the door, but as insiders who need continuous supervision and adaptive containment. It is the first major enterprise vendor to build this layer.

The original Project Perception, previewed in August , was designed to defend against external threats using red, blue, and green agent teams. The October update turns that architecture inward. The new framing: agents are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems, and that access creates insider risk — not because agents are malicious, but because they can make mistakes, be manipulated, or drift from their assigned task as context changes.

The product details are specific. Guardian Agents provide continuous, machine-speed supervision of every agent action, investigating risk changes and recommending or applying containment. Dynamic Agent Risk calculates a continuously updated risk score by combining signals from identity, data, endpoints, cloud, network, runtime, and the agent’s own activity — including chain-of-thought analysis for intent drift. Dynamic Conditional Access extends Microsoft Entra so that a risk change triggers graduated responses: the system might preserve read access while blocking writes, narrow the data an agent can reach, require provable human approval for a consequential step, or isolate the runtime entirely. And Dynamic Permissions ensures agents start with zero authority and receive only task-scoped, time-bound access.

Satya Nadella framed the principle plainly: “The most trustworthy agentic system will not be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one designed that enables us to trust the model least.”

Microsoft has expanded agent discovery to 60 supported local types — up from 25 — including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot. Entra Agent ID, which reached general availability in April 2026, has been extended with identity types for local and previously unknown agents discovered through security sensors. The whole stack is bundled into Microsoft 365 E7 at $99 per user per month , which packages E5, Copilot, Entra Suite, and Agent 365.

This follows a 27-day sprint in which three major vendors shipped agent security products. Okta launched Agent SSO on September 22. ServiceNow introduced AI Passport on October 15. Microsoft followed on October 19. The identity perimeter that began forming in late September now has a containment layer sitting on top of it.

But the measurement gap has not closed. The Okta AI Agents at Work 2026 survey found 96% of executives confident in their identity and access management for non-human identities, yet only 34% actually apply the same controls they use for human employees. The Saviynt CISO AI Risk Report 2026 found 92% of CISOs lack full visibility into AI agent identities. And the NIST AI Risk Management Framework MEASURE function — the part that would tell you whether an agent’s actions align with its intended purpose — scored 0.6 out of 5.0, rated critical.

Terrell Cox, Microsoft’s Corporate Vice President and Deputy CISO, offered the candid version: “As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats.”

The question is not whether containment matters — it does, and Microsoft is first to build it at enterprise scale. The question is what containment cannot tell you. Dynamic Agent Risk can stop an agent from doing damage. It can narrow permissions in real time, require human approval, or kill the runtime. What it cannot yet tell you is whether the agent is actually doing its job correctly — whether the expense it approved was the right call, whether the code it wrote matches the spec, whether the research it produced is accurate. That is the measurement layer, and it still does not exist.

The $99 per user per month price tag also raises a practical question about who gets access to this kind of containment. If agent security becomes a premium bundle feature, smaller enterprises and budget-constrained teams will be making do with less — at exactly the moment when agents are proliferating fastest.

facts.text: We introduced Project Perception and the Microsoft cyber stack to help organizations defend with agents.
Today, we are extending Perception to secure the agentic insider .

Guardian Agents help security teams operate continuously, at machine speed and scale, while sensors, context, and actuators across the cyber stack help understand changing agent risk and continuously adapt protection in response.
Agents can be created through Microsoft platforms, integrated through partner platforms and software development kits (SDKs), or introduced locally without a central deployment process.
An agent should not be free to call any tool, API, Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, resource, or other agent it can find.
Local and network and data controls must mediate those paths, observe the calls, and enforce enterprise policy.
Controlling the destination alone is not enough.
Security must also understand the content flowing into and out of the agent, including its sensitivity, provenance, and whether untrusted data may be influencing the agent’s behavior.
Agents are rapidly becoming part of how work gets done.
They can support a range of activities from writing code and researching products to analyzing revenue, processing expenses, and acting across the systems that run the business.
To be most useful, they often need access to company data, applications, tools, and other agents.
That access is what makes agents more capable.

Satya Nadella, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Microsoft, recently described the trust architecture this new era requires: we must separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.
We should not ask a model to be its own security authority.
The controls that determine what it can access, what actions it can take, and whether it should continue operating must sit outside the model, where the model cannot bypass or tamper with them.
The security system must be able to understand what changed and act before a person can manually investigate every signal.
This means an agent can become a policy target even when it was not originally integrated with Microsoft Security.
Sandboxes such as Microsoft Execution Container (MXC) provide policy-controlled access to resources the agent needs to complete its task.
Agents will only be adopted at scale if they can be trusted at scale.
At Microsoft, we are already operating in a world of hundreds of thousands of agents.

As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats.
Those lessons directly inform the innovations we are delivering to help every organization adopt agents with confidence.”
— Terrell Cox, Corporate Vice President (CVP) and Deputy Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), Customer Security, Microsoft
That requires a clear division of responsibility.
Independent controls establish identity, limit privilege, protect data, preserve evidence, and contain unsafe action.
Security continuously reassesses risk and adapts protection as the agent works.
Protect your people, data, and infrastructure with AI-powered, end-to-end security from Microsoft.
Greater model transparency gives security systems deeper evidence to detect suspicious behavior and inform Dynamic Agent Risk.

Agents make those principles even more important.
Dynamic Conditional Access extends Microsoft Entra Conditional Access for agents so a change in risk can drive coordinated action across multiple enforcement points.
Securing agents must itself become agentic, while remaining inside boundaries people set.

extraction.body: Technology and Science updated 3h ago 2 min read This article is an automated aggregation of coverage from news outlets. Our editorials offer in-depth analysis curated by the NewsCord team. TorchNeuron runs PyTorch code on Trainium with a single configuration change. Challenges Nvidia's software and hardware dominance in AI compute. Amazon Web Services launched TorchNeuron, a software tool meant to let developers run code written in PyTorch on Amazon’s Trainium chips with just one configuration change, without rewriting existing applications. Colin Brace, vice president of software at Annapurna Labs, said the initiative was intended to simplify the process of testing and adopting Amazon’s in-house chips, telling Reuters, “This has been about meeting customers where they're at.” Amazon said it would unveil the software at a developer conference in Silicon Valley on Monday and release it publicly as a free, open-source offering, positioning the move as an alternative to Nvidia’s AI computing technology. TorchNeuron compiles via PyTorch XLA path and AWS Neuron Amazon’s pitch centered on Nvidia’s CUDA software platform, which Nvidia has spent more than a decade developing and refining to enable PyTorch-based applications to run efficiently on its chips. Amazon also said more than 30 early customers across fields including robotics, world models and voice AI were already using the new software. TorchNeuron had been in private betas since late last year, and Amazon opened the software to all developers as a public beta on Monday. Colin Brace told GeekWire, “If you know PyTorch, then you know Trainium,” as he described how TorchNeuron changes the process from modifying code to a basic configuration change. Amazon planned to release TorchNeuron as open-source software on Tuesday in conjunction with the PyTorch Conference in San Jose, Calif., and Brace said Amazon’s goal was wide use of the chips. extraction.body: (Oct 19): Bitcoin popped back above US$82,000 on Monday, rebounding with risk assets as oil prices declined. The original cryptocurrency climbed as much as 2.3% in early Asia trading and was hovering around US$82,400 at noon in Singapore. Smaller tokens also advanced. Ether was up as much as 3.7%, while solana gained more than 4.6%. Cryptocurrencies have joined a tentative recovery in risk appetite after oil retreated from a five-month high on signs that supplies from the Middle East have held up since the US war with Iran broke out. Brent crude fell as much as 2%, while a gauge of S&P 500 futures was up roughly 0.8% and Nasdaq 100 futures were up 1.3%. Improving macro conditions have helped bitcoin reverse its trend from last week, when it fell roughly 3% along with a selloff in stocks led by technology shares amid renewed doubts about massive spending on artificial intelligence. Today’s move higher is a “retracement after a big risk-off week”, said Damien Loh, chief investment officer at Ericsenz Capital. “No news is good news,” he said. “I don’t see any near-term drivers for it to break new highs, and I think the risk is for the downside given overall risk environment.” Oil remains elevated at roughly US$107 a barrel, higher than prices for most of last week. Institutional demand has also pulled back from bitcoin for two consecutive weeks. US-listed spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds recorded US$228.6 million (RM933.3 million) in outflows last week following US$681 million in outflows the previous week. Bitcoin remains within last week’s trading range of US$80,000 to US$85,000. Copyright © 1999- 2026 The Edge Communications Sdn. Bhd. 199301012242 (266980-X). All rights reserved

extraction.body: (Oct 19): Bitcoin popped back above US$82,000 on Monday, rebounding with risk assets as oil prices declined. The original cryptocurrency climbed as much as 2.3% in early Asia trading and was hovering around US$82,400 at noon in Singapore. Smaller tokens also advanced. Ether was up as much as 3.7%, while solana gained more than 4.6%. Cryptocurrencies have joined a tentative recovery in risk appetite after oil retreated from a five-month high on signs that supplies from the Middle East have held up since the US war with Iran broke out. Brent crude fell as much as 2%, while a gauge of S&P 500 futures was up roughly 0.8% and Nasdaq 100 futures were up 1.3%. Improving macro conditions have helped bitcoin reverse its trend from last week, when it fell roughly 3% along with a selloff in stocks led by technology shares amid renewed doubts about massive spending on artificial intelligence. Today’s move higher is a “retracement after a big risk-off week”, said Damien Loh, chief investment officer at Ericsenz Capital. “No news is good news,” he said. “I don’t see any near-term drivers for it to break new highs, and I think the risk is for the downside given overall risk environment.” Oil remains elevated at roughly US$107 a barrel, higher than prices for most of last week. Institutional demand has also pulled back from bitcoin for two consecutive weeks. US-listed spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds recorded US$228.6 million (RM933.3 million) in outflows last week following US$681 million in outflows the previous week. Amazon is now serving up its first notable discounts on Apple’s M4 Mac mini lineup of 2026 . All three of the configurations it offers were on sale for Black Friday for a little bit less ($20 less to be exact), as well as on and off in the lead up to Christmas 2025, but we are otherwise looking at some solid discounts here and the best we have tracked over the last few weeks since. On the two 16GB variants above, you’re essentially looking at some of the lowest prices we tracked across all of 2025, save for the bonus $20 in savings during Black Friday and a couple short-lived dips previous to that. The 16GB/512GB config in particular is now matching the lowest we have tracked at Amazon outside of the $670 Black Friday offer. Much of this applies to the 24GB/512GB model list above, but that one did see a few particularly notable discounts in May and early June of last year that had it down as low as $842 at Amazon for a short time. All of that said, for me the Mac mini is already well worth its price of entry before the discounts, is the most value-packed Apple purchase I have made personally in the last year or two, and I truly cannot recommend it enough for folks looking towards a relatively affordable Apple desktop experience. And just for reference, Apple Watch Ultra 3 is starting at $774 on Amazon right now. While we did see a very short-lived offer on Cyber Monday only that delivered a new all-time low on Apple’s entry-level iPad mini 7 models , deals are not often any better than $100 off the list prices. This is the same offer we had been tracking for the holidays last year and into 2026, but Amazon has slashed an additional $10 off some of the most affordable models for $110 in savings . Amazon is now offering Apple’s latest base model iPad mini (A17 Pro) starting from $389.99 shipped . Regularly $499, you’re looking at nearly $110 in savings here on the Blue and Starlight models – the other two are still at $399. Again we did see a mostly one-day offer at $150 off, but anything lower than $100 off is notable on this machine and today we are getting a little bonus savings. Much like we mentioned last go around, if you have some Amazon gift cards in the holster from the holidays, you might actually be able to land the lowest price ever on one of this miniature Apple tablets. All things considered, this is sort of a lot of iPad for $390. That is perhaps an odd way to put it being this is Apple’s tiniest model, it is the most affordable model that supports Apple Intelligence and I happen to think of it as one of the best couch browsers or travel tablet companions out there. I’d $499 is a fair list price, and $390 is a pretty sweet deal here. Just for comparison’s sake, Best Buy is still offering these machines at $100 off , or $10 more than Amazon’s best deals. sources.title: Apple’s last-gen Mac Mini with the M4 is $150 off

extraction.body: Best Buy has a great deal for the rest of the day on the M4 Mac Mini base model that has 16GB RAM and a 256GB SSD. Normally, it doesn’t make a ton of sense to buy the M4 model for its usual $799 price given that the newer, faster M6 version has been available from Amazon for $779.99 (originally $899) for the past couple of weeks. The M4 Mac Mini launched at $599 in 2024, and was an incredible value. Their design and ports are nearly identical, and with either model you’ll need to supply your own keyboard, mouse, display, webcam, etc. If you’re on the fence and can’t decide between the M4 and M6 models, I suggest checking out my colleague Antonio’s review of the M6 Mac Mini. The newer model might be well worth the extra $130 cost. Read our review of the M4 Mac Mini and the M6 Mac Mini More Verge-approved deals * Today brought a big discount to LG’s C6 OLEDs lineup, particularly its bigger models. The 55-inch model is $999.99 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Costco (previously $1,399.99), costing a little less than the 42- and 48-inch configurations. The 65-inch model is cheaper than before, too. Previously $1,699.99, but normally selling for $1,500 or so, you can grab the larger version for $1,399.99 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Costco. If you have a big room and budget, the 77-inch LG C6H that, like the 48-inch version, has a tandem OLED panel that offers more brightness and better colors, is $1,999.99, down from $2,499.99. * For $499.99, you can grab a 14-inch HP OmniBook 3 during Best Buy’s deal of the day that has a 2K OLED screen, a capable Snapdragon X ARM processor, 16GB of RAM, and a 256GB SSD. Its Snapdragon processor can run most x86 Windows 11 apps without much issue, and it’s just a rarity to get these kinds of specs — from the OLED screen to the RAM amount — at $500. My colleague Antonio reviewed the 16-inch version that cuts some corners in the screen department compared to this 14-inch model. * It’s time to get spooky if you haven’t already planned your run of games for Halloween. The spectacular Silent Hill 2 remake is down to $21.34 on Steam for PC via Fanatical, a third-party site I’ve shopped from numerous times. If you’re alright with spending more, Resident Evil Requiem is one of Capcom’s several great 2026 games, and it’s $20 off at Amazon on all platforms, costing $49.99.

extraction.body: Best Buy has a great deal for the rest of the day on the M4 Mac Mini base model that has 16GB RAM and a 256GB SSD. Normally, it doesn’t make a ton of sense to buy the M4 model for its usual $799 price given that the newer, faster M6 version has been available from Amazon for $779.99 (originally $899) for the past couple of weeks. The M4 Mac Mini launched at $599 in 2024, and was an incredible value. Their design and ports are nearly identical, and with either model you’ll need to supply your own keyboard, mouse, display, webcam, etc. If you’re on the fence and can’t decide between the M4 and M6 models, I suggest checking out my colleague Antonio’s review of the M6 Mac Mini. The newer model might be well worth the extra $130 cost. Read our review of the M4 Mac Mini and the M6 Mac Mini More Verge-approved deals * Today brought a big discount to LG’s C6 OLEDs lineup, particularly its bigger models. The 55-inch model is $999.99 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Costco (previously $1,399.99), costing a little less than the 42- and 48-inch configurations. The 65-inch model is cheaper than before, too. Previously $1,699.99, but normally selling for $1,500 or so, you can grab the larger version for $1,399.99 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Costco. If you have a big room and budget, the 77-inch LG C6H that, like the 48-inch version, has a tandem OLED panel that offers more brightness and better colors, is $1,999.99, down from $2,499.99. * For $499.99, you can grab a 14-inch HP OmniBook 3 during Best Buy’s deal of the day that has a 2K OLED screen, a capable Snapdragon X ARM processor, 16GB of RAM, and a 256GB SSD. Its Snapdragon processor can run most x86 Windows 11 apps without much issue, and it’s just a rarity to get these kinds of specs — from the OLED screen to the RAM amount — at $500. My colleague Antonio reviewed the 16-inch version that cuts some corners in the screen department compared to this 14-inch model. * It’s time to get spooky if you haven’t already planned your run of games for Halloween. The spectacular Silent Hill 2 remake is down to $21.34 on Steam for PC via Fanatical, a third-party site I’ve shopped from numerous times. If you’re alright with spending more, Resident Evil Requiem is one of Capcom’s several great 2026 games, and it’s $20 off at Amazon on all platforms, costing $49.99.

passages: Tenstorrent is part of a wave of AI hardware startups trying to chip away at Nvidia’s dominance.
Among them is Etched, an AI chip maker that was fielding investment offers at valuations of $40 billion or more, TechCrunch reported earlier this month.
The new capital will go toward scaling chips tailored for serving open-weight AI models and video generation.
Tenstorrent, a chip startup focused on inference, has raised $1.5 billion at a $6.2 billion valuation.

The fresh round, which more than doubled Tenstorrent’s valuation from the $2.6 billion it fetched in late 2024, was led by Trace Capital, a new firm launched by Quiet Capital co-founder Ben Mahdavi, and Innovation X.
Other backers included Cadence Ventures, Eclipse, Fidelity, SanDisk, and T.

sources.title: Tenstorrent Hits $6.2B Valuation in $1.5B AI Chip Round
passages: Tenstorrent, the open-weight AI chip startup, just closed a $1.5 billion funding round at a $6.2 billion valuation, choosing independence over acquisition after drawing serious buyer interest earlier this year.
Tenstorrent just became one of the most valuable private AI chip companies on the planet.
Earlier in 2026, Tenstorrent drew acquisition interest from multiple strategic buyers, according to the TechCrunch report.
The clustering of mega-rounds at stratospheric valuations reflects investor conviction that AI infrastructure is still in early innings, with room for multiple platforms to scale.
That's created an opening for companies like Tenstorrent, which is betting that open-weight architectures will win over customers tired of proprietary constraints.
That decision signals confidence that the market for AI chips is big enough to support multiple winners, and that Tenstorrent's open approach can carve out meaningful share.
While Nvidia's chips require developers to work within its CUDA framework, Tenstorrent's architecture is designed to be more accessible and customizable.
