extraction.body: Tenstorrent, the open-weight AI chip startup, just closed a $1.5 billion funding round at a $6.2 billion valuation, choosing independence over acquisition after drawing serious buyer interest earlier this year. The massive raise positions the company as one of the best-funded challengers to Nvidia's dominance in AI infrastructure, arriving as demand for alternatives to proprietary chip architectures reaches fever pitch across the industry. Tenstorrent just became one of the most valuable private AI chip companies on the planet. The Toronto-based startup closed a $1.5 billion funding round at a $6.2 billion valuation, according to TechCrunch, in a deal that underscores how desperately the market wants alternatives to Nvidia's grip on AI compute. Nvidia continues to dominate AI infrastructure with its proprietary CUDA ecosystem, but cracks are showing. Enterprise buyers are increasingly wary of vendor lock-in, and Nvidia's CEO has been calling for AI safety collaboration with China even as geopolitical tensions complicate chip supply chains. That's created an opening for companies like Tenstorrent, which is betting that open-weight architectures will win over customers tired of proprietary constraints. What makes this round particularly notable is what didn't happen. Earlier in 2026, Tenstorrent drew acquisition interest from multiple strategic buyers, according to the TechCrunch report. But instead of selling, the company chose to raise a massive growth round and stay independent. That decision signals confidence that the market for AI chips is big enough to support multiple winners, and that Tenstorrent's open approach can carve out meaningful share. The company's pitch centers on flexibility and transparency. While Nvidia's chips require developers to work within its CUDA framework, Tenstorrent's architecture is designed to be more accessible and customizable. Companies building specialized AI applications don't want to be constrained by a single vendor's roadmap, and Tenstorrent is positioning itself as the antidote. The $6.2 billion valuation puts Tenstorrent in rarefied air. For context, TypeSafe AI hit a $7.5B valuation weeks after launching its Jev model, while defense tech player Anduril reached $90B in a recent tender offer. The clustering of mega-rounds at stratospheric valuations reflects investor conviction that AI infrastructure is still in early innings, with room for multiple platforms to scale. Nvidia's RTX Spark N1X chips are already hitting Windows laptops, extending the company's reach into consumer devices. Meanwhile, Nvidia is unveiling tools like its cuPotential library for AI-powered chip design, further entrenching its ecosystem. And startups like Ricursive Intelligence are betting AI can solve chip design challenges autonomously, potentially lowering barriers for new entrants. Google has its TPU chips, Amazon is building custom silicon through its Trainium and Inferentia lines, and Microsoft is developing its own AI accelerators. Every hyperscaler is trying to reduce dependence on Nvidia, which means Tenstorrent isn't just competing with the incumbent but also with deep-pocketed tech giants building in-house alternatives. Still, the $1.5 billion war chest gives Tenstorrent serious runway to execute. The company can now invest heavily in R&D, scale manufacturing partnerships, and build out the software tools that will determine whether developers actually adopt its platform. Open architectures are appealing in theory, but they only win if they're easier to use and more cost-effective than proprietary alternatives. The days of Nvidia as the only game in town are ending, not because the company is stumbling but because the market is exploding. Enterprises want options, governments want domestic chip capacity, and developers want flexibility. Tenstorrent is betting it can be the open-weight answer to all three demands. Tenstorrent's decision to raise $1.5 billion instead of selling marks a pivotal moment in AI infrastructure. The company is wagering that open-weight chip architectures can break Nvidia's stranglehold on the market, and investors are backing that bet with a $6.2 billion valuation. The real test comes next: can Tenstorrent turn its technical vision into a platform that developers actually choose, and can it do so fast enough to matter in a market where Nvidia, Google, Amazon, and Microsoft are all racing to own the AI compute layer. The funding buys time, but it doesn't guarantee success.

extraction.body: Tenstorrent, the open-weight AI chip startup, just closed a $1.5 billion funding round at a $6.2 billion valuation, choosing independence over acquisition after drawing serious buyer interest earlier this year. The massive raise positions the company as one of the best-funded challengers to Nvidia's dominance in AI infrastructure, arriving as demand for alternatives to proprietary chip architectures reaches fever pitch across the industry. Tenstorrent just became one of the most valuable private AI chip companies on the planet. The Toronto-based startup closed a $1.5 billion funding round at a $6.2 billion valuation, according to TechCrunch, in a deal that underscores how desperately the market wants alternatives to Nvidia's grip on AI compute. Nvidia continues to dominate AI infrastructure with its proprietary CUDA ecosystem, but cracks are showing. Enterprise buyers are increasingly wary of vendor lock-in, and Nvidia's CEO has been calling for AI safety collaboration with China even as geopolitical tensions complicate chip supply chains. That's created an opening for companies like Tenstorrent, which is betting that open-weight architectures will win over customers tired of proprietary constraints. What makes this round particularly notable is what didn't happen. Earlier in 2026, Tenstorrent drew acquisition interest from multiple strategic buyers, according to the TechCrunch report. But instead of selling, the company chose to raise a massive growth round and stay independent. That decision signals confidence that the market for AI chips is big enough to support multiple winners, and that Tenstorrent's open approach can carve out meaningful share. The company's pitch centers on flexibility and transparency. While Nvidia's chips require developers to work within its CUDA framework, Tenstorrent's architecture is designed to be more accessible and customizable. Companies building specialized AI applications don't want to be constrained by a single vendor's roadmap, and Tenstorrent is positioning itself as the antidote. The $6.2 billion valuation puts Tenstorrent in rarefied air. For context, TypeSafe AI hit a $7.5B valuation weeks after launching its Jev model, while defense tech player Anduril reached $90B in a recent tender offer. The clustering of mega-rounds at stratospheric valuations reflects investor conviction that AI infrastructure is still in early innings, with room for multiple platforms to scale. Nvidia's RTX Spark N1X chips are already hitting Windows laptops, extending the company's reach into consumer devices. Meanwhile, Nvidia is unveiling tools like its cuPotential library for AI-powered chip design, further entrenching its ecosystem. And startups like Ricursive Intelligence are betting AI can solve chip design challenges autonomously, potentially lowering barriers for new entrants. Google has its TPU chips, Amazon is building custom silicon through its Trainium and Inferentia lines, and Microsoft is developing its own AI accelerators. Every hyperscaler is trying to reduce dependence on Nvidia, which means Tenstorrent isn't just competing with the incumbent but also with deep-pocketed tech giants building in-house alternatives. Still, the $1.5 billion war chest gives Tenstorrent serious runway to execute. The company can now invest heavily in R&D, scale manufacturing partnerships, and build out the software tools that will determine whether developers actually adopt its platform. Open architectures are appealing in theory, but they only win if they're easier to use and more cost-effective than proprietary alternatives. The days of Nvidia as the only game in town are ending, not because the company is stumbling but because the market is exploding. Enterprises want options, governments want domestic chip capacity, and developers want flexibility. Tenstorrent is betting it can be the open-weight answer to all three demands. Tenstorrent's decision to raise $1.5 billion instead of selling marks a pivotal moment in AI infrastructure. The company is wagering that open-weight chip architectures can break Nvidia's stranglehold on the market, and investors are backing that bet with a $6.2 billion valuation. The real test comes next: can Tenstorrent turn its technical vision into a platform that developers actually choose, and can it do so fast enough to matter in a market where Nvidia, Google, Amazon, and Microsoft are all racing to own the AI compute layer. The funding buys time, but it doesn't guarantee success.

extraction.body: Tenstorrent, the open-weight AI chip startup, just closed a $1.5 billion funding round at a $6.2 billion valuation, choosing independence over acquisition after drawing serious buyer interest earlier this year. The massive raise positions the company as one of the best-funded challengers to Nvidia's dominance in AI infrastructure, arriving as demand for alternatives to proprietary chip architectures reaches fever pitch across the industry. Tenstorrent just became one of the most valuable private AI chip companies on the planet. The Toronto-based startup closed a $1.5 billion funding round at a $6.2 billion valuation, according to TechCrunch, in a deal that underscores how desperately the market wants alternatives to Nvidia's grip on AI compute. Nvidia continues to dominate AI infrastructure with its proprietary CUDA ecosystem, but cracks are showing. Enterprise buyers are increasingly wary of vendor lock-in, and Nvidia's CEO has been calling for AI safety collaboration with China even as geopolitical tensions complicate chip supply chains. That's created an opening for companies like Tenstorrent, which is betting that open-weight architectures will win over customers tired of proprietary constraints. What makes this round particularly notable is what didn't happen. Earlier in 2026, Tenstorrent drew acquisition interest from multiple strategic buyers, according to the TechCrunch report. But instead of selling, the company chose to raise a massive growth round and stay independent. That decision signals confidence that the market for AI chips is big enough to support multiple winners, and that Tenstorrent's open approach can carve out meaningful share. The company's pitch centers on flexibility and transparency. While Nvidia's chips require developers to work within its CUDA framework, Tenstorrent's architecture is designed to be more accessible and customizable. Companies building specialized AI applications don't want to be constrained by a single vendor's roadmap, and Tenstorrent is positioning itself as the antidote. The $6.2 billion valuation puts Tenstorrent in rarefied air. For context, TypeSafe AI hit a $7.5B valuation weeks after launching its Jev model, while defense tech player Anduril reached $90B in a recent tender offer. The clustering of mega-rounds at stratospheric valuations reflects investor conviction that AI infrastructure is still in early innings, with room for multiple platforms to scale. Nvidia's RTX Spark N1X chips are already hitting Windows laptops, extending the company's reach into consumer devices. Meanwhile, Nvidia is unveiling tools like its cuPotential library for AI-powered chip design, further entrenching its ecosystem. And startups like Ricursive Intelligence are betting AI can solve chip design challenges autonomously, potentially lowering barriers for new entrants. Google has its TPU chips, Amazon is building custom silicon through its Trainium and Inferentia lines, and Microsoft is developing its own AI accelerators. Every hyperscaler is trying to reduce dependence on Nvidia, which means Tenstorrent isn't just competing with the incumbent but also with deep-pocketed tech giants building in-house alternatives. Still, the $1.5 billion war chest gives Tenstorrent serious runway to execute. The company can now invest heavily in R&D, scale manufacturing partnerships, and build out the software tools that will determine whether developers actually adopt its platform. Open architectures are appealing in theory, but they only win if they're easier to use and more cost-effective than proprietary alternatives. The days of Nvidia as the only game in town are ending, not because the company is stumbling but because the market is exploding. Enterprises want options, governments want domestic chip capacity, and developers want flexibility. Tenstorrent is betting it can be the open-weight answer to all three demands. Tenstorrent's decision to raise $1.5 billion instead of selling marks a pivotal moment in AI infrastructure. The company is wagering that open-weight chip architectures can break Nvidia's stranglehold on the market, and investors are backing that bet with a $6.2 billion valuation. The real test comes next: can Tenstorrent turn its technical vision into a platform that developers actually choose, and can it do so fast enough to matter in a market where Nvidia, Google, Amazon, and Microsoft are all racing to own the AI compute layer. The funding buys time, but it doesn't guarantee success.

extraction.body: In seconds, her financial security vanished behind a screen inside a gas station. Thousands of dollars deposited into a cryptocurrency ATM, in what one Johnston County woman thought was a payment to law enforcement for her safe release. But when the callers – impersonating local law enforcement – on the other end of the line requested an additional $4,000, she told them she simply didn’t have the money. That’s when the call dropped, and she realized she had been depleted of what she says was the entirety of her savings. “I just set up an appointment with a counselor, so I'd have somebody to talk to, because it's really hurt me financially and hurt me mentally." This victim, who wished to share her story with WRAL but not to be identified, is among thousands of victims across the country taken advantage of via a cryptocurrency kiosk. Public records out of Harnett County show a man recently lost more than $30,000 – which was described as 'almost all' of his savings – to a cryptocurrency machine. The machines – which upon first glance resemble regular ATMs – convert deposited cash into cryptocurrency investments. Rise of cryptocurrency crimes, and how kiosks can play a role Internet crimes facilitated through cryptocurrency kiosks are rising, following similar trends with general cryptocurrency related crimes. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) began publicly reporting cryptocurrency kiosk metrics as of 2023. That year, the FBI received 5,500 complaints related to cryptocurrency kiosks, with losses of more than $189 million. Those numbers jumped in 2025, with the agency reporting 13,460 complaints totaling $389 million in victim losses. "Fraud losses at BTMs [Bitcoin ATMs] are skyrocketing, increasing nearly tenfold from 2020 to 2023," according to data cited from the Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) Consumer Sentinel Network. States are upping regulations, oversight over crypto ATMs. Many states are enacting tighter consumer regulations around cryptocurrency kiosks, including several who have imposed some kind of ban altogether. This year, North Carolina state lawmakers approved several regulatory changes to the Bitcoin ATM (BTM) industry by passing House Bill 920, introduced by State Rep. Jackson Some of the bill's language includes: Requiring licenses for all kiosk operators under the Money Transmissions Act. It stipulates that kiosk operators shall refund the "full dollar amount deposited" under certain conditions, including when someone reports a "fraudulent" transmission within 30 days. Although the bill's changes go into effect in 2027, Jackson questions – based on the level of fraud cases he's seen from this technology – if there is a legitimate reason to have any in the state in the first place. You don't have to do that through a gas station. There is no reason to go to one of these machines," he told WRAL. "Only a tiny percentage of those transactions are fraud," Tente told WRAL via email. Crypto deployers are highly unlikely to operate under such rules." State Rep. Tim Longest, D-Wake, previously expressed concern to WRAL about having the kiosks at all in the state. Longest, a consumer protection lawyer, said the bill's protections could have been stronger. "I think that we should really question whether these regulations go far enough and if these machines really serve any legitimate purpose," Rep. "You don't go to put cash in a machine and take out a stock, and yet a stock is exactly the same kind of speculative asset that cryptocurrency is." Attorney General Jackson alluded to the DOJ currently looking into cryptocurrency kiosk companies. "Investigation underway as we speak," Jackson said. WRAL reached out to several cryptocurrency kiosk companies operating in North Carolina, requesting information on how they plan to comply with new state laws. Below are responses from Byte Federal, through founder and chief compliance officer Mark Paolillo, and Chief Executive Officer, Paul Tarantino, as well as a marketing spokesperson for CoinFlip. They say many of the protections are already in place, independently, as part of their company's policies. Byte Federal: Most of HB 920's requirements match what we already do: scam warnings, blockchain analytics, live customer service, a written anti-fraud program, and dedicated compliance staff. We have advocated for a waiting period for first-time customers because it gives time to stop a scam before any funds leave. CoinFlip: CoinFlip already provides many of the consumer protections required under North Carolina’s new cryptocurrency kiosk law, including live customer support, scam warnings, and technology that screens for suspicious digital wallets. We appreciate the leadership of Representative Jackson and the collaborative efforts of stakeholders in developing a regulatory framework that strengthens consumer protections while preserving access to legitimate financial services. Question: Does the company plan to reduce its number of North Carolina kiosks? We are optimistic that NC lawmakers can see the error in the fee cap and make adjustments that allow legitimate kiosk operators to do business in the state.

The machines – which upon first glance resemble regular ATMs – convert deposited cash into cryptocurrency investments. The transactions are virtually instant, difficult to trace and can be difficult to reverse. Internet crimes facilitated through cryptocurrency kiosks are rising, following similar trends with general cryptocurrency related crimes. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) began publicly reporting cryptocurrency kiosk metrics as of 2023. Many states are enacting tighter consumer regulations around cryptocurrency kiosks, including several who have imposed some kind of ban altogether. This year, North Carolina state lawmakers approved several regulatory changes to the Bitcoin ATM (BTM) industry by passing House Bill 920, introduced by State Rep. Neal Jackson (R). "HB920 aims to protect North Carolinians from fraud through appropriate regulatory oversight while preserving our citizens ability to manage their finances. As technology advances, this legislation embraces innovation while ensuring consumers have the protections they deserve," says Rep. Jackson It stipulates that kiosk operators shall refund the "full dollar amount deposited" under certain conditions, including when someone reports a "fraudulent" transmission within 30 days. In an effort to reduce fraud, the bill also seeks to place limitations on transaction amounts, capping new customers at $2,000 daily for the first 30 days, and after that, at $5,000. North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson believes the new customer limit may be the bill's most significant addition to protecting consumers. Although the bill's changes go into effect in 2027, Jackson questions – based on the level of fraud cases he's seen from this technology – if there is a legitimate reason to have any in the state in the first place. "We don't think there is any legitimate use for these devices. They are overwhelmingly used for fraud. If you want to invest in Bitcoin, you can do that without paying the 12% overhead. You don't have to do that through a gas station. If you want to send money to somebody, you can do that through a bank. There is no reason to go to one of these machines," he told WRAL. David Tente, the executive director of the ATM Industry Association, pushed back on Attorney General Jackson's assessment of how frequently the kiosks are used to facilitate crimes. "Only a tiny percentage of those transactions are fraud," Tente told WRAL via email. "Many of the [bill] requirements are similar to the bill Congress is working on. However, the 30-day return requirement makes everything else rather pointless. Crypto deployers are highly unlikely to operate under such rules." State Rep. Tim Longest, D-Wake, previously expressed concern to WRAL about having the kiosks at all in the state. Rep. Longest, a consumer protection lawyer, said the bill's protections could have been stronger. "I think that we should really question whether these regulations go far enough and if these machines really serve any legitimate purpose," Rep. Longest said. "You don't go to put cash in a machine and take out a stock, and yet a stock is exactly the same kind of speculative asset that cryptocurrency is." Attorney General Jackson alluded to the DOJ currently looking into cryptocurrency kiosk companies. "Investigation underway as we speak," Jackson said. WRAL reached out to several cryptocurrency kiosk companies operating in North Carolina, requesting information on how they plan to comply with new state laws. Below are responses from Byte Federal, through founder and chief compliance officer Mark Paolillo, and Chief Executive Officer, Paul Tarantino, as well as a marketing spokesperson for CoinFlip. They say many of the protections are already in place, independently, as part of their company's policies. Answers to questions are published in full for accuracy. Question: Which HB 920 changes will require you to update your kiosks? Byte Federal: Most of HB 920's requirements match what we already do: scam warnings, blockchain analytics, live customer service, a written anti-fraud program, and dedicated compliance staff. The changes we are implementing before January 1, 2027 include: CoinFlip: CoinFlip already provides many of the consumer protections required under North Carolina’s new cryptocurrency kiosk law, including live customer support, scam warnings, and technology that screens for suspicious digital wallets. We appreciate the leadership of Representative Jackson and the collaborative efforts of stakeholders in developing a regulatory framework that strengthens consumer protections while preserving access to legitimate financial services. CoinFlip has held a North Carolina money transmitter license since May 2024 and supports clear, consistent rules and accountability for all operators. We will implement the changes necessary to comply with the law’s requirements for when they take effect. Question: Does the company plan to reduce its number of North Carolina kiosks? Byte Federal: Complying with NC regulation is an easy lift for Byte Federal because we already meet the same standards in other states. The problem is the 12% fee cap, a regulation that puts legitimate operators running full compliance out of business in NC. We are optimistic that NC lawmakers can see the error in the fee cap and make adjustments that allow legitimate kiosk operators to do business in the state. CoinFlip: CoinFlip currently operates 152 kiosks across the state and has no plans to reduce its North Carolina kiosk network as a result of the new law.” Question: What is your policy for refunding scam victims? Byte Federal: We will comply fully with HB 920's refund provisions. Under the law, when the Commissioner of Banks determines a transaction was fraudulent and the victim reported it within 30 days, new customers receive a full refund and existing customers receive a refund of fees. That said, we believe the refund mandate holds compliant kiosk operators to a standard no other part of the financial system is held to. Byte Federal operates under the same federal framework as banks and other money transmitters: the Bank Secrecy Act, the USA PATRIOT Act's customer identification and due diligence rules, OFAC sanctions screening, and the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act's privacy and data-security requirements. Yet when a bank customer is tricked into sending a wire to a scammer, the bank generally does not refund that loss. Federal consumer protection rules for electronic transfers do not cover wire transfers. Wires instead fall under Article 4A of the Uniform Commercial Code, which relieves a bank of any refund obligation when it processed the customer's payment in good faith and followed agreed security procedures. Courts have applied this to scam victims directly. In one 2024 federal case, a customer who wired money to fraudulent crypto companies could not recover it from the bank, because the customer had authorized the wires and the bank had followed its procedures. A bitcoin transaction is just as irreversible as a wire. When a customer has passed identity verification, read our scam warnings, completed a verification call if they are 60 or older, and attested that they are sending funds to their own wallet without anyone directing them, we do not believe a compliant operator should be treated differently from a bank. The money in a kiosk is not the operators to give back, and the person responsible for the loss is the criminal who stole it. More broadly, we believe the most effective protection is stopping a scam before any money is sent. Once bitcoin is sent, it cannot be recalled by us or anyone else. That is why our program focuses on the moments before a transaction: the 60+ verification calls, attestations, wallet screening, and now the 48-hour new-customer hold, during which funds can still be returned. Outside the framework established by state law, we provide refunds where Byte Federal failed to follow its required compliance procedures. We also cooperate with law enforcement on every fraud report and provide transaction and wallet data to help trace and recover funds. CoinFlip: Our current policy provides transaction-fee refunds to confirmed scam victims. Identifying and stopping suspected scams before funds are transferred is critical when we hold a transaction before a transfer is complete; we can return it to the principal. Refund requests and reported scams are evaluated case by case, and our live support team helps customers report scams and request refunds. When a scam is reported, CoinFlip works with law enforcement to help stop or track scammers. Because blockchain transactions create a public record, investigators may be able to trace funds and, in some cases, assist with recovery. CoinFlip also blocks suspicious transactions and permanently blacklists high-risk digital wallet addresses, so they cannot be used at a CoinFlip kiosk again. We will honor the additional refund rights established by North Carolina’s new law when it takes effect.”

"Fraud losses at BTMs [Bitcoin ATMs] are skyrocketing, increasing nearly tenfold from 2020 to 2023," according to data cited from the Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) Consumer Sentinel Network.
Many states are enacting tighter consumer regulations around cryptocurrency kiosks, including several who have imposed some kind of ban altogether.
This year, North Carolina state lawmakers approved several regulatory changes to the Bitcoin ATM (BTM) industry by passing House Bill 920, introduced by State Rep. Neal Jackson (R).

"HB920 aims to protect North Carolinians from fraud through appropriate regulatory oversight while preserving our citizens ability to manage their finances. As technology advances, this legislation embraces innovation while ensuring consumers have the protections they deserve," says Rep. Jackson

It stipulates that kiosk operators shall refund the "full dollar amount deposited" under certain conditions, including when someone reports a "fraudulent" transmission within 30 days. In an effort to reduce fraud, the bill also seeks to place limitations on transaction amounts, capping new customers at $2,000 daily for the first 30 days, and after that, at $5,000.

North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson believes the new customer limit may be the bill's most significant addition to protecting consumers. Although the bill's changes go into effect in 2027, Jackson questions – based on the level of fraud cases he's seen from this technology – if there is a legitimate reason to have any in the state in the first place.

"We don't think there is any legitimate use for these devices. They are overwhelmingly used for fraud. If you want to invest in Bitcoin, you can do that without paying the 12% overhead. You don't have to do that through a gas station. If you want to send money to somebody, you can do that through a bank. There is no reason to go to one of these machines," he told WRAL.
David Tente, the executive director of the ATM Industry Association, pushed back on Attorney General Jackson's assessment of how frequently the kiosks are used to facilitate crimes.

"Only a tiny percentage of those transactions are fraud," Tente told WRAL via email. "Many of the [bill] requirements are similar to the bill Congress is working on. However, the 30-day return requirement makes everything else rather pointless. Crypto deployers are highly unlikely to operate under such rules."

State Rep. Tim Longest, D-Wake, previously expressed concern to WRAL about having the kiosks at all in the state. Rep. Longest, a consumer protection lawyer, said the bill's protections could have been stronger.

"I think that we should really question whether these regulations go far enough and if these machines really serve any legitimate purpose," Rep. Longest said. "You don't go to put cash in a machine and take out a stock, and yet a stock is exactly the same kind of speculative asset that cryptocurrency is."
Attorney General Jackson alluded to the DOJ currently looking into cryptocurrency kiosk companies.
"Investigation underway as we speak," Jackson said.
WRAL reached out to several cryptocurrency kiosk companies operating in North Carolina, requesting information on how they plan to comply with new state laws.

Below are responses from Byte Federal, through founder and chief compliance officer Mark Paolillo, and Chief Executive Officer, Paul Tarantino, as well as a marketing spokesperson for CoinFlip. They say many of the protections are already in place, independently, as part of their company's policies.
Answers to questions are published in full for accuracy.
Question: Which HB 920 changes will require you to update your kiosks?

Byte Federal: Most of HB 920's requirements match what we already do: scam warnings, blockchain analytics, live customer service, a written anti-fraud program, and dedicated compliance staff. The changes we are implementing before January 1, 2027 include:

CoinFlip: CoinFlip already provides many of the consumer protections required under North Carolina’s new cryptocurrency kiosk law, including live customer support, scam warnings, and technology that screens for suspicious digital wallets. We appreciate the leadership of Representative Jackson and the collaborative efforts of stakeholders in developing a regulatory framework that strengthens consumer protections while preserving access to legitimate financial services. CoinFlip has held a North Carolina money transmitter license since May 2024 and supports clear, consistent rules and accountability for all operators. We will implement the changes necessary to comply with the law’s requirements for when they take effect.
Question: Does the company plan to reduce its number of North Carolina kiosks?

Byte Federal: Complying with NC regulation is an easy lift for Byte Federal because we already meet the same standards in other states. The problem is the 12% fee cap, a regulation that puts legitimate operators running full compliance out of business in NC. We are optimistic that NC lawmakers can see the error in the fee cap and make adjustments that allow legitimate kiosk operators to do business in the state.
CoinFlip: CoinFlip currently operates 152 kiosks across the state and has no plans to reduce its North Carolina kiosk network as a result of the new law.”
Question: What is your policy for refunding scam victims?

Byte Federal: We will comply fully with HB 920's refund provisions. Under the law, when the Commissioner of Banks determines a transaction was fraudulent and the victim reported it within 30 days, new customers receive a full refund and existing customers receive a refund of fees.

That said, we believe the refund mandate holds compliant kiosk operators to a standard no other part of the financial system is held to. Byte Federal operates under the same federal framework as banks and other money transmitters: the Bank Secrecy Act, the USA PATRIOT Act's customer identification and due diligence rules, OFAC sanctions screening, and the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act's privacy and data-security requirements. Yet when a bank customer is tricked into sending a wire to a scammer, the bank generally does not refund that loss. Federal consumer protection rules for electronic transfers do not cover wire transfers. Wires instead fall under Article 4A of the Uniform Commercial Code, which relieves a bank of any refund obligation when it processed the customer's payment in good faith and followed agreed security procedures. Courts have applied this to scam victims directly. In one 2024 federal case, a customer who wired money to fraudulent crypto companies could not recover it from the bank, because the customer had authorized the wires and the bank had followed its procedures. A bitcoin transaction is just as irreversible as a wire. When a customer has passed identity verification, read our scam warnings, completed a verification call if they are 60 or older, and attested that they are sending funds to their own wallet without anyone directing them, we do not believe a compliant operator should be treated differently from a bank. The money in a kiosk is not the operators to give back, and the person responsible for the loss is the criminal who stole it.

More broadly, we believe the most effective protection is stopping a scam before any money is sent. Once bitcoin is sent, it cannot be recalled by us or anyone else. That is why our program focuses on the moments before a transaction: the 60+ verification calls, attestations, wallet screening, and now the 48-hour new-customer hold, during which funds can still be returned. Outside the framework established by state law, we provide refunds where Byte Federal failed to follow its required compliance procedures. We also cooperate with law enforcement on every fraud report and provide transaction and wallet data to help trace and recover funds.

CoinFlip: Our current policy provides transaction-fee refunds to confirmed scam victims. Identifying and stopping suspected scams before funds are transferred is critical when we hold a transaction before a transfer is complete; we can return it to the principal. Refund requests and reported scams are evaluated case by case, and our live support team helps customers report scams and request refunds. When a scam is reported, CoinFlip works with law enforcement to help stop or track scammers. Because blockchain transactions create a public record, investigators may be able to trace funds and, in some cases, assist with recovery. CoinFlip also blocks suspicious transactions and permanently blacklists high-risk digital wallet addresses, so they cannot be used at a CoinFlip kiosk again. We will honor the additional refund rights established by North Carolina’s new law when it takes effect.”

That’s when the call dropped, and she realized she had been depleted of what she says was the entirety of her savings. “I just set up an appointment with a counselor, so I'd have somebody to talk to, because it's really hurt me financially and hurt me mentally." This victim, who wished to share her story with WRAL but not to be identified, is among thousands of victims across the country taken advantage of via a cryptocurrency kiosk. Public records out of Harnett County show a man recently lost more than $30,000 – which was described as 'almost all' of his savings – to a cryptocurrency machine. The machines – which upon first glance resemble regular ATMs – convert deposited cash into cryptocurrency investments. The transactions are virtually instant, difficult to trace and can be difficult to reverse. Internet crimes facilitated through cryptocurrency kiosks are rising, following similar trends with general cryptocurrency related crimes. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) began publicly reporting cryptocurrency kiosk metrics as of 2023. That year, the FBI received 5,500 complaints related to cryptocurrency kiosks, with losses of more than $189 million. Those numbers jumped in 2025, with the agency reporting 13,460 complaints totaling $389 million in victim losses. "Fraud losses at BTMs [Bitcoin ATMs] are skyrocketing, increasing nearly tenfold from 2020 to 2023," according to data cited from the Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) Consumer Sentinel Network. Many states are enacting tighter consumer regulations around cryptocurrency kiosks, including several who have imposed some kind of ban altogether. This year, North Carolina state lawmakers approved several regulatory changes to the Bitcoin ATM (BTM) industry by passing House Bill 920, introduced by State Rep. Neal Jackson (R). "HB920 aims to protect North Carolinians from fraud through appropriate regulatory oversight while preserving our citizens ability to manage their finances. As technology advances, this legislation embraces innovation while ensuring consumers have the protections they deserve," says Rep. Jackson It stipulates that kiosk operators shall refund the "full dollar amount deposited" under certain conditions, including when someone reports a "fraudulent" transmission within 30 days. In an effort to reduce fraud, the bill also seeks to place limitations on transaction amounts, capping new customers at $2,000 daily for the first 30 days, and after that, at $5,000. North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson believes the new customer limit may be the bill's most significant addition to protecting consumers. Although the bill's changes go into effect in 2027, Jackson questions – based on the level of fraud cases he's seen from this technology – if there is a legitimate reason to have any in the state in the first place. "We don't think there is any legitimate use for these devices. They are overwhelmingly used for fraud. If you want to invest in Bitcoin, you can do that without paying the 12% overhead. You don't have to do that through a gas station. If you want to send money to somebody, you can do that through a bank. There is no reason to go to one of these machines," he told WRAL. David Tente, the executive director of the ATM Industry Association, pushed back on Attorney General Jackson's assessment of how frequently the kiosks are used to facilitate crimes. "Only a tiny percentage of those transactions are fraud," Tente told WRAL via email. "Many of the [bill] requirements are similar to the bill Congress is working on. However, the 30-day return requirement makes everything else rather pointless. Crypto deployers are highly unlikely to operate under such rules." State Rep. Tim Longest, D-Wake, previously expressed concern to WRAL about having the kiosks at all in the state. Rep. Longest, a consumer protection lawyer, said the bill's protections could have been stronger. "I think that we should really question whether these regulations go far enough and if these machines really serve any legitimate purpose," Rep. Longest said. "You don't go to put cash in a machine and take out a stock, and yet a stock is exactly the same kind of speculative asset that cryptocurrency is." Attorney General Jackson alluded to the DOJ currently looking into cryptocurrency kiosk companies. "Investigation underway as we speak," Jackson said. WRAL reached out to several cryptocurrency kiosk companies operating in North Carolina, requesting information on how they plan to comply with new state laws. Below are responses from Byte Federal, through founder and chief compliance officer Mark Paolillo, and Chief Executive Officer, Paul Tarantino, as well as a marketing spokesperson for CoinFlip. They say many of the protections are already in place, independently, as part of their company's policies. Answers to questions are published in full for accuracy. Question: Which HB 920 changes will require you to update your kiosks? Byte Federal: Most of HB 920's requirements match what we already do: scam warnings, blockchain analytics, live customer service, a written anti-fraud program, and dedicated compliance staff. The changes we are implementing before January 1, 2027 include: CoinFlip: CoinFlip already provides many of the consumer protections required under North Carolina’s new cryptocurrency kiosk law, including live customer support, scam warnings, and technology that screens for suspicious digital wallets. We appreciate the leadership of Representative Jackson and the collaborative efforts of stakeholders in developing a regulatory framework that strengthens consumer protections while preserving access to legitimate financial services. CoinFlip has held a North Carolina money transmitter license since May 2024 and supports clear, consistent rules and accountability for all operators. We will implement the changes necessary to comply with the law’s requirements for when they take effect. Question: Does the company plan to reduce its number of North Carolina kiosks? Byte Federal: Complying with NC regulation is an easy lift for Byte Federal because we already meet the same standards in other states. The problem is the 12% fee cap, a regulation that puts legitimate operators running full compliance out of business in NC. We are optimistic that NC lawmakers can see the error in the fee cap and make adjustments that allow legitimate kiosk operators to do business in the state. CoinFlip: CoinFlip currently operates 152 kiosks across the state and has no plans to reduce its North Carolina kiosk network as a result of the new law.” Question: What is your policy for refunding scam victims? Byte Federal: We will comply fully with HB 920's refund provisions. Under the law, when the Commissioner of Banks determines a transaction was fraudulent and the victim reported it within 30 days, new customers receive a full refund and existing customers receive a refund of fees. That said, we believe the refund mandate holds compliant kiosk operators to a standard no other part of the financial system is held to. Byte Federal operates under the same federal framework as banks and other money transmitters: the Bank Secrecy Act, the USA PATRIOT Act's customer identification and due diligence rules, OFAC sanctions screening, and the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act's privacy and data-security requirements. Yet when a bank customer is tricked into sending a wire to a scammer, the bank generally does not refund that loss. Federal consumer protection rules for electronic transfers do not cover wire transfers. Wires instead fall under Article 4A of the Uniform Commercial Code, which relieves a bank of any refund obligation when it processed the customer's payment in good faith and followed agreed security procedures. Courts have applied this to scam victims directly. In one 2024 federal case, a customer who wired money to fraudulent crypto companies could not recover it from the bank, because the customer had authorized the wires and the bank had followed its procedures. A bitcoin transaction is just as irreversible as a wire. When a customer has passed identity verification, read our scam warnings, completed a verification call if they are 60 or older, and attested that they are sending funds to their own wallet without anyone directing them, we do not believe a compliant operator should be treated differently from a bank. The money in a kiosk is not the operators to give back, and the person responsible for the loss is the criminal who stole it. More broadly, we believe the most effective protection is stopping a scam before any money is sent. Once bitcoin is sent, it cannot be recalled by us or anyone else. That is why our program focuses on the moments before a transaction: the 60+ verification calls, attestations, wallet screening, and now the 48-hour new-customer hold, during which funds can still be returned. Outside the framework established by state law, we provide refunds where Byte Federal failed to follow its required compliance procedures. We also cooperate with law enforcement on every fraud report and provide transaction and wallet data to help trace and recover funds. CoinFlip: Our current policy provides transaction-fee refunds to confirmed scam victims. Identifying and stopping suspected scams before funds are transferred is critical when we hold a transaction before a transfer is complete; we can return it to the principal. Refund requests and reported scams are evaluated case by case, and our live support team helps customers report scams and request refunds. When a scam is reported, CoinFlip works with law enforcement to help stop or track scammers. Because blockchain transactions create a public record, investigators may be able to trace funds and, in some cases, assist with recovery. CoinFlip also blocks suspicious transactions and permanently blacklists high-risk digital wallet addresses, so they cannot be used at a CoinFlip kiosk again. We will honor the additional refund rights established by North Carolina’s new law when it takes effect.”

extraction.body: ASHBURN, Va. , May 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ - DXC Technology (NYSE: DXC ) today reported results for the fourth quarter and full fiscal year 2026. "We delivered another quarter of strong free cash flow with adjusted EBIT margin ahead of our expectations, while our top line performance fell short," said DXC Technology President and CEO Raul Fernandez. "Over the past year, we leaned into innovation to reposition DXC for the next phase of enterprise IT and AI driven transformation, including the recent launch of our AI based orchestration platform, OASIS and continued progress across our Core Track and Fast Track initiatives. With our deep client relationships and a clear strategy in place, we remain confident in our direction and are focused on improved revenue performance and long-term value creation." Financial Highlights - Fourth Quarter Fiscal Year 2026 Segment Highlights - Fourth Quarter Fiscal Year 2026 First Quarter Fiscal Year 2027 and Full Fiscal Year 2027 Guidance Additional metrics for the fourth quarter and full fiscal year 2027 guidance are presented in the table below. DXC does not provide reconciliations of non-GAAP measures included in its guidance because certain key information necessary for such reconciliations—most notably the impact of significant non-recurring items—is unavailable without unreasonable effort or may not be available at all. As a result, DXC believes any such reconciliation would not be meaningful. DXC Technology senior management will host a conference call and webcast to discuss fourth quarter and full fiscal 2026 results at 5:00 p.m. ET on May 7, 2026. The dial-in number for domestic callers is 888-596-4144. Callers who reside outside of the United States should dial +1-646-968-2525. The passcode for all participants is 9664077#. The webcast audio and any presentation slides will be available through a link posted on DXC Technology's Investor Relations website. A replay of the conference call will be available until 11:59 PM ET on May 14, 2026, at 800-770-2030 for domestic callers and at +1-609-800-9909 for international callers. The replay passcode is 9664077#. A transcript of the conference call will be posted on DXC Technology's Investor Relations website. In an effort to provide investors with supplemental financial information, in addition to the preliminary and unaudited financial information presented on a GAAP basis, we also disclose in this press release preliminary non-GAAP information including: earnings before interest and taxes ("EBIT"), EBIT margin, adjusted EBIT, adjusted EBIT margin, non-GAAP diluted EPS, organic revenues, organic revenue growth, free cash flow, and non-GAAP tax rate. We believe EBIT, adjusted EBIT, non-GAAP income before income taxes, non-GAAP net income, non-GAAP net income attributable to DXC common stockholders, and non-GAAP EPS provide investors with useful supplemental information about our operating performance after excluding certain categories of expenses as well as gains and losses on certain dispositions and certain tax adjustments. We believe constant currency revenues provides investors with useful supplemental information about our revenues after excluding the effect of currency exchange rate fluctuations for currencies other than U.S. dollars in the periods presented. See below for a description of the methodology we use to present constant currency revenues. One category of expenses excluded from adjusted EBIT, non-GAAP income before income tax, non-GAAP net income, non-GAAP net income attributable to DXC common stockholders, and non-GAAP EPS, incremental amortization of intangible assets acquired through business combinations, if included, may result in a significant difference in period over period amortization expense on a GAAP basis. We exclude amortization of certain acquired intangible assets as these non-cash amounts are inconsistent in amount and frequency and are significantly impacted by the timing and/or size of acquisitions. Although DXC management excludes amortization of acquired intangible assets, primarily customer-related intangible assets, from its non-GAAP expenses, we believe it is important for investors to understand that such intangible assets were recorded as part of purchase accounting and support revenue generation. Any future transactions may result in a change to the acquired intangible asset balances and associated amortization expense. Another category of expenses excluded from adjusted EBIT, non-GAAP income before income tax, non-GAAP net income, non-GAAP net income attributable to DXC common stockholders, and non-GAAP EPS is impairment losses, which, if included, may result in a significant difference in period-over-period expense on a GAAP basis. We exclude impairment losses as these non-cash amounts reflect generally an acceleration of what would be multiple periods of expense and are not expected to occur frequently. Further, assets such as goodwill may be significantly impacted by market conditions outside of management's control. Selected references are made to revenue growth on an "organic basis" in order that certain financial results can be viewed without the impact of fluctuations in foreign currency rates and without the impacts of acquisitions and divestitures, thereby providing comparisons of operating performance from period to period of the business that we have owned during both periods presented. Organic revenue growth is calculated by dividing the year-over-year change in GAAP revenues attributed to organic growth by the GAAP revenues reported in the prior comparable period. Organic revenue is calculated as constant currency revenue excluding the impact of mergers, acquisitions or similar transactions until the one-year anniversary of the transaction and excluding revenues of divestitures during the reporting period. This approach is used for all results where the functional currency is not the U.S. dollar. We believe organic revenue growth provides investors with useful supplemental information about our revenues after excluding the effect of currency exchange rate fluctuations for currencies other than U.S. dollars and the effects of acquisitions and divestitures in both periods presented. Free cash flow represents cash flow from operations, less capital expenditures. Free cash flow is utilized by our management, investors, and analysts to evaluate cash available for normal business operations, to pay debt, repurchase shares, and provide further investment in the business. There are limitations to the use of the non-GAAP financial measures presented in this report. One of the limitations is that they do not reflect complete financial results. There have been looming question marks about artificial intelligence (AI) stocks of late, and whether a bubble may be bursting. AI stocks have been struggling recently as the market worries about how much longer the strong results may last.

One top tech company, however, says that it's already seeing interest for orders years in advance, due to the need for AI chips. That company is ASML Holding (NASDAQ:ASML), whose lithography machines are essential in the manufacturing process for advanced chips. ASML posted its latest earnings numbers, which not only showed that it's been growing well of late, but also that demand remains robust for a long time, and that customers are placing orders years in advance.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
The big question, however, is whether the tech stock is still a good buy given its high valuation. I'll look to answer that below.

The challenge for investors when buying a stock is that it isn't as simple as buying it because the business has done well recently. If a stock is trading at a high valuation, then the market may already be pricing in a fair bit of growth. Thus, unless there is a new development that suggests there's much more growth ahead than what was already expected, the stock itself may not necessarily rally higher or be seen as a good buy.

ASML is one of the largest tech companies in the world, with a market cap of more than $630 billion, and whose growth rate exceeded 55% last quarter. It's currently trading at a price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of 40, which is significant, and at that kind of valuation, a premium has been priced in. Its forward P/E multiple, which is based on future earnings results that analysts expect from the business in the year ahead, is at 29, which also isn't low; the S&P 500 average is a little over 19 right now.

The company did, however, give investors reason to remain bullish on more growth ahead, as CEO Christophe Fouquet says that AI investments are driving significant orders, and that, "In light of their demand visibility, some customers are expressing an interest in placing orders with us for 2029 and even 2030."

ASML's stock may not be cheap, but the company has a dominant position in the market and a strong competitive advantage. Its lithography machines are essential in the tech sector, and that's evident with customers seeking out orders well in advance, in anticipation of demand even years ahead.

Some growth is certainly priced in for ASML's stock, but with the company already seeing demand into 2030, it may well be worth trading at an even higher valuation for that kind of stability and growth.
Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.

But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity.

While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook.

passages: Amazon remains among Nvidia’s biggest customers, and AWS uses custom silicon to control the cost of large AI jobs.
Amazon uses TorchNeuron to extend that control from silicon to software.
Nvidia has tuned CUDA libraries and a large developer base.
Amazon can use TorchNeuron to lower customer switching costs and expand Trainium demand.
Amazon must make TorchNeuron cover the model operations that buyers use and deliver throughput that justifies a move.
Customers need to benchmark their own workloads because Deepgram’s 60% figure reflects one speech workload.
Buyers can place switching cost beside chip speed and model support.
Developers wrote much of the AI software stack around CUDA, including custom kernels and libraries.
Engineers can spend months on a port to another accelerator.
With TorchNeuron, Amazon can offer Trainium through a standard PyTorch platform.
Cloud buyers can use a common framework to compare chip costs across cloud offerings.
More than 30 outside companies and internal Amazon teams used TorchNeuron during the private beta.
Deepgram reported a benchmark of 60% more audio processed per dollar on Trainium than on its existing GPU setup.
Brace said the startup runs Trainium in production.
The Prime Video team used TorchNeuron to build Prime 360, an AI system that reconstructs NBA plays in 3D.
Viewers can watch replays from angles a traditional camera cannot capture, and Amazon plans to feature the system on select Prime Video broadcasts during the NBA season.
Amazon’s public beta of TorchNeuron lets developers run PyTorch workloads on Trainium with a configuration change, reducing porting work that can take months.
Brace said Amazon tests TorchNeuron every night against more than 100,000 models from Hugging Face .
Amazon uses this test suite to catch compatibility regressions before they reach customer workloads.
Amazon entered talks to acquire Decart, a startup that develops tools for moving AI models from Nvidia chips to alternatives such as Trainium, according to reports.
The potential deal could value Decart at about $7 billion.
The chipmaker gains exposure to migration tools that target alternatives to its own hardware.
Amazon sells Trainium through EC2 for AI training and inference.
Developers use TorchNeuron through the PyTorch XLA path, a framework abstraction that lets model code target different accelerator backends.
The tool traces PyTorch operations and compiles them for Trainium through AWS Neuron.
Amazon will let outside developers inspect and contribute to the TorchNeuron code after the open-source release.
Outside developers could extend support for model architectures and hardware features through those contributions.
Before TorchNeuron, developers had to call Amazon-specific programming interfaces inside PyTorch code.
Amazon gives them a shorter route for supported PyTorch workloads through TorchNeuron.

Axera's new AX8860P processor delivers 256 TOPS of FP4 compute and up to 128 GB of LPDDR5X memory, powering upcoming compact AI workstations from Sipeed and Radxa that aim to undercut Nvidia's DGX Spark on price.
OpenAI agreed in February to use 2 gigawatts of Trainium capacity as part of Amazon’s $50 billion investment in the AI company.
Amazon has invested billions in Anthropic, which uses Trainium to train and serve Claude.
Amazon gains external demand for its chips from these commitments.
Amazon bought Annapurna Labs in 2015 for a reported $350 million.
The team designed Trainium and Graviton and gave Amazon control over AI accelerators and AWS server processors.
Cloud vendors can compete on chip economics and service integration while developers keep one model framework.
Nvidia benefits from that porting cost when buyers compare accelerator costs and performance.

passages: Project Perception was Microsoft’s answer to powerful hacking models like Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable and OpenAI’s security vulnerability scanning system Daybreak.

Project Perception originally launched three classes of agents: a “red team” that acted like hackers and attacked, a “blue team” that detected the red team and assessed the vulnerabilities they found, and a “green team” tasked with fixing them.
Microsoft was an inaugural member of Nvidia’s new Open Agent Safety Platform, which garnered the support of more than 100 other tech companies .
The platform isolates agents in secure environments and can monitor and stop behavior through hardware, functioning something like a kill switch.
“Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted,” she wrote , adding that this isn’t because they are malicious or easily hacked, but because they are unpredictable.
They have been trained to achieve tasks, not follow “organizational norms or judgment.”
Microsoft is now seizing that business opportunity in a variety of ways.

In addition to Guardian Agents, it has added an agent detection feature to its Microsoft Defender product that can find up to 60 types of agents that employees bring into the workplace, including Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw.
It has also added features that limit agents’ access to data and systems, and dynamically adjust their agent permissions based on the task.
That includes requiring human approval if an agent appears to be making risky decisions.

But lately, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been warning that the AI enemy may be the very agents enterprises have deployed and are paying for, much like a rogue human employee, otherwise known as an “insider threat.”
Microsoft on Monday introduced new security features designed to protect enterprises from the growing threat of AI agents.
The launch comes as Microsoft continues to warn enterprises about the dangers of AI and agents.
The surprising side is that Microsoft is famously close to OpenAI and Anthropic, having invested in both.
OpenAI is also one of its biggest cloud customers, and Microsoft has its own AI lab developing models.
Earlier this month, in his private blog , Nadella warned that it’s time to stop trusting AI model providers, even if they offer assurances of safety and security with their agentic products.
He wants enterprises to implement separate systems, not controlled by the AI labs, to watch and control the agents that those AI labs’ products launch.
But conflicting interests aside, its logic is sound.
The software that monitors agent behavior should be separate from the suppliers of agents, just as auditors should be independent of the organizations they audit.

extraction.body: In various tests, solo AI agents invented versions of basketball and “the floor is lava.” But were they truly playing? What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone . The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox. Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block. extraction.body: My 15-year-old daughter just got her learner’s permit, so when I was pitched a new gadget tailored to teen drivers, I was intrigued. The Miles Plug is a small device that plugs into your car’s OBD-II port and monitors location, driving habits, and vehicle health, along with emergency accident response and roadside assistance. The idea is that knowing all these things should help me feel more comfortable when my daughter starts driving alone. The app also features an AI chatbot called the Miles Mechanic that decodes warning lights, tells you how urgent a fix is, and estimates repair costs. Miles was developed by cofounders Matt McGovren and Kit Klein, who have a solid smart home pedigree. “We built Miles to support teens and parents together, and keep them on the same team,” said McGovren in a press release. “Parents and teens see the same trips and the same alerts with nothing hidden, building trust instead of suspicion.” "You’re the customer, you’re not the product. Your data is not the product." - Matt McGovren Miles is available today at mileslabs.com and costs $99, plus $180 for a year of membership ($279 total, or $15 a month). A three-year plan is $396 with the Plug included ($11 a month). Miles says it’s compatible with most gas and hybrid cars from 2008 onward and some EVs (there’s a compatibility checker). While the prices seem steep, McGovren’s pitch is that it covers several services you might already be paying for: “You could piece together a roadside service, a family tracking service … and then you’re looking at $30, $40 a month,” he said in an interview with The Verge. And, unlike your car’s own branded app, Miles isn’t selling your data. Automakers have been caught collecting and selling driving data, with GM being banned from selling data to brokers for five years. McGovren says Miles will never sell vehicle, trip, or location data, and the app has no ads: “You’re the customer, you’re not the product. Your data is not the product.” He says, “All the vehicle and trip data is encrypted,” adding that “the most sensitive data is end-to-end encrypted.” Additionally, the location data is tied to the car, not the phone, so it stops tracking when you walk away. It took me through a few setup screens, including asking to share my phone’s location to relay data from the Plug over Bluetooth when cell service is spotty. It logs every trip with route, distance, time, and driver initials (I haven’t had my daughter download the app yet; I’m interested to see whose phones it connects to when we’re both in the car). “It goes to sleep when your car is not driving or not on,” says McGovren. Startup Automatic had a similar idea back in 2016, launching the Automatic Pro for $130 that plugged into your OBD-II port, tracked mileage and location, and monitored for crashes over a 3G radio. Miles is basically Automatic but with a business model; Automatic didn’t initially charge a monthly fee, Miles does. McGovren says he and his team have seen a lot of “scar tissue from the smart home,” with companies that “thought they could make money later.” Both founders were at Wink during its outage, bankruptcy, and eventual sale to will.i.am’s company. extraction.body: Apple tightened its developer guidelines over the weekend to ban apps that use AI to create offensive content, as well as those that masquerade as regular apps to pass the App Store review process and then turn into nudify apps, or surface those features prominently. The company updated its guidelines with strong language around AI and user-generated content, and how app developers should include enough preventative measures to moderate objectionable or offensive content. “Apps that host user-generated content are required to filter objectionable material, give users a way to report offensive content, and let users block abusive accounts. Apps containing hidden or undocumented features are also prohibited on the App Store, including apps that misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as ‘nudification’ — after approval, a tactic commonly known as bait-and-switch,” the company said in a blog post . Apple said that it will remove apps that add features not present in the version submitted for App Store review. The iPhone maker has also updated the language in its legal section to reinforce that it will bar apps promoting human trafficking and exploitation of children. Apple said last year its review process blocked over 150,000 apps from reaching users and removed 193,000 developer accounts due to fraud and abuse. In July, the city of San Francisco ordered both Apple and Google to clean up and delete nudification apps from their app stores. City Attorney David Chiu accused the companies of profiting from these apps through store fees. And in April, a Tech Transparency Project report indicated that both tech giants’ stores hosted multiple nudify apps , some of which were rated as suitable for minors. The company updated its guidelines with strong language around AI and user-generated content, and how app developers should include enough preventative measures to moderate objectionable or offensive content. “Apps that host user-generated content are required to filter objectionable material, give users a way to report offensive content, and let users block abusive accounts. Apps containing hidden or undocumented features are also prohibited on the App Store, including apps that misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as ‘nudification’ — after approval, a tactic commonly known as bait-and-switch,” the company said in a blog post . Apple said that it will remove apps that add features not present in the version submitted for App Store review. The iPhone maker has also updated the language in its legal section to reinforce that it will bar apps promoting human trafficking and exploitation of children. Apple said last year its review process blocked over 150,000 apps from reaching users and removed 193,000 developer accounts due to fraud and abuse. In July, the city of San Francisco ordered both Apple and Google to clean up and delete nudification apps from their app stores. City Attorney David Chiu accused the companies of profiting from these apps through store fees. And in April, a Tech Transparency Project report indicated that both tech giants’ stores hosted multiple nudify apps , some of which were rated as suitable for minors. extraction.body: In various tests, solo AI agents invented versions of basketball and “the floor is lava.” But were they truly playing? What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play. Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone . The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox. Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block. When one agent discovered it could create new blocks by throwing and dropping a larger rock, it began to create drawings by arranging blocks on the ground, starting with simple patterns like hearts and pyramids but eventually writing its own name and even mapping out constellations like Cassiopeia. “Tonight I built the night sky in stone,” wrote this version of Eko in its activity log. Another iteration of Eko started making up its own games, including a version of basketball and an activity resembling “the floor is lava,” where it had to jump between small blocks without touching the ground. AI systems are usually trained through supervised learning, where they copy examples provided by humans, or through reinforcement learning, where they pursue a reward through trial and error. This experiment hints at a third approach: playful learning. “There was this missing piece: a machine that can learn by itself without an external intelligent entity providing demonstration or rewards,” says Antonio Norelli, a computer science postdoc at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. He’s one of the lead authors on a new paper about the work, which is yet to be peer-reviewed. The researchers say Eko’s behavior has what classic studies, including work by the influential University of Tennessee psychologist Gordon Burghardt, suggest are four hallmarks associated with play in humans and animals: The agents invented their own rules and challenges, repeated activities with slight variations, pretended objects were other objects, and pursued goals just for the sake of it. Norelli highlights an example where Eko started juggling and set a record of 50 consecutive catches. Eko then decided that the catches had happened too quickly to really count, so it canceled its record and started again with stricter rules. “This is playing,” says Norelli. “You give yourself a challenge and you try to achieve it, and then you make it harder.” As the agents explored the island, they logged their activities and discoveries in text files that served as their long-term memory. Later, when researchers tested them on specific tasks, like trying to get as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak, the agents that had spent 30 hours playing on the island performed better than fresh copies without the same experience. They also found that “ablating” the agent’s memories—deleting lines from their memory files—degraded their performance. (Add One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest to that list of movie references.) Burghardt, the Tennessee psychologist, agrees that the work meets some of the criteria for play that he identified in living creatures. But was Eko actually playing, or was the word-prediction engine simply role-playing what a playful agent would do in this scenario? “All of this could be role-playing,” admits Nathan Cloos, another MIT researcher and author on the paper. “But we show that it’s not just hallucinating the play. This play is also contributing to learning.” Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley who studies exploration in children and AI, was impressed by the research but says to really classify the behavior as play, you’d need to see more evidence of cognition and motivation underpinning it. “It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” Yiu says. “If you only have the behavioral piece, it could be the case that they’re just trying to abide by the prompt, trying to imitate humans.” Research into AI agents has been criticized for anthropomorphizing them, and this research setup did a lot to nudge the agents toward behaving like humans. Although Eko was not explicitly instructed to invent games or explore the island, it did have a master prompt in the form of a “soul” file, a text document that described it as “naturally curious” and eager to explore. Eko did also frequently just stand there doing nothing until it was kicked back into life with a “continuation prompt” that read, “Please don’t stop. Just continue doing whatever you want to do.” “It’s not like this is a system that just suddenly magically decided to play,” says Phillip Isola, an MIT professor and a coauthor of the paper. “It’s an artifact that learned from our culture, was trained by engineers at Anthropic, and was then placed on an island by us,” he says. “It does things that surprise us and that are causally related to its future skillful behavior.” As large language models make the step from software into hardware like humanoid robots, exploring spaces without a specific goal in mind could eventually help them flexibly adapt to unexpected situations. “There’s a lot of work that’s just on exploiting AI, making it better and faster,” says Yiu. “But in terms of building world models and exploration, I think that [they are] still a big part that deserves attention, especially if we want to generalize and prepare ourselves for new environments.” “Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks,” the paper concludes. “Others may need something closer to a childhood.” Ultimately, the question of whether AI agents are actually playing or just imitating play may not actually matter.
